purpose:
The Mayor has pledged in his manifesto to
“Arrange a Winter Ice Rink in the town centre – to
support local businesses and offer residents and visitors an
additional activity in the town.”
The project aims to enhance the festive offer, increase footfall,
support local businesses, and provide an inclusive seasonal
experience for residents and visitors.
The rink will cost approximately £300,000, inclusive of a 20%
contingency.
The Mace Foundation has agreed to sponsor the event jointly with
WBC on a 50/50 cost sharing basis. A Memorandum of Understanding is
currently being prepared to formalise its sponsorship
commitment.
WBC will fund its 50% share using CIL. £150,000
All ticket sales revenue—estimated at £128,000 based on
current revenue modelling—will be allocated to charitable
organisation(s) jointly selected by the Mace Foundation and
WBC.
This report is to agree the allocation of WBC CIL monies to fund
50% of the costs.

purpose:
Watford Borough Council is commissioning a
permanent public artwork in honour of the late Margaret Maughan,
Great Britain’s first Paralympic gold medallist and a
long-term Watford resident. Located within the new Riverwell
Square, the artwork will celebrate Margaret’s remarkable
life, achievements and legacy, while creating a lasting public
tribute in a prominent and accessible civic space. The commission
will also contribute to the quality, identity and cultural value of
the Riverwell development, providing residents, visitors and future
generations with a meaningful focal point for reflection, pride and
inspiration. WBC will allocate £50,000 of CIL funding to
support the delivery of this sculpture commission.

purpose:
Sale of property, 122 Exchange Road, to New
Hope
content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Senior Regeneration Manager which sought
approval for the disposal of 122 Exchange Road.  It was noted that the appendices were exempt from
publication, as they contained commercially sensitive information,
in accordance with Paragraph 3 of Part 1 of Schedule 12A of the
Local Government Act 1972.
 
The
Mayor commented that there had been lots of discussions with New
Hope.  The organisation provided several
important services on many sites in Watford.  This proposal would enable them to consolidate
services in a purpose-built facility. 
He invited Councillor Hill to provide further details.
 
Councillor Hill advised that consideration had been given to the
best outcome of this surplus site and how it could be
used.  It worked well sitting alongside
New Hope’s neighbouring site.  It
was recognised the offer was below the appraised
valuation.  However, the site would be
difficult to develop due to its location.  Proceeds from the sale to New Hope would be ring
fenced for affordable housing.
 
Councillor Pattinson said that this proposal supported the
council’s vision, particularly as it sat alongside the
Housing Strategy that had been approved earlier in the
meeting.  It was a step towards
delivering the council’s housing ambition, ensuring assets
were used to make a positive difference.  It would create high quality temporary
accommodation.  It provided the most
vulnerable with safe and stable accommodation as well as health
support.  Temporary accommodation was a
lifeline for people facing crisis.  It
would help them to move on to more settled accommodation as soon as
possible.  This was a prudent decision,
improving lives, and was an example of good financial stewardship,
using public resources for the best possible outcome.
 
Councillor Bell recognised this was a co-ordinated approach
towards homelessness.  He welcomed the
joined up approach and supported the proposal.
 
Councillor Dychton commented that, as a Central ward councillor,
the property was in a central location. 
She was pleased it would be going ahead and supporting the
homelessness strategy.  She was aware
that some residents had raised some concerns.  However, the organisation had good engagement
plans, providing good communication to residents.
 
The
Mayor thanked everyone for their comments.  In the past there had been problems, but New Hope,
the council and residents had worked together.  New Hope was clear that it wanted to be good
neighbour to the residents and local businesses.  This project would improve the provision by New
Hope.  He thanked officers for the work,
as he was aware of the discussions that had taken place to get to
this point.
 
There
were no questions or comments about the information contained in
the appendices, the Mayor invited members to vote on the
recommendations.
 
Resolved –
 

1.      that the disposal of 122
Exchange Road to New Hope for a sum of £200,000, being less
than best consideration, is agreed.

 

2.      that the Director of
Regeneration and Growth and Section 151 Officer, in consultation
with the Mayor and the Portfolio Holder for Property, Resources and
Customer Services and the Portfolio Holder for Finance, is
authorised to agree the final form of legal agreements to be
entered into by the council.

 

3.      that Cabinet agrees to
ring-fencing the proceeds of this disposal towards the delivery of
more temporary and affordable housing within the
Borough.
topline: The Council has decided to approve the disposal of a property to New Hope for the creation of a purpose-built facility to support vulnerable individuals in Watford.

purpose:
This report sets out the revenue and capital
year end position for the financial year 2025/26. The position is
subject to external audit and may change.
content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Chief Finance Officer which provided the
year end Financial Monitoring Report for 2025/26.  The minutes had also been provided from Finance
Scrutiny Committee which had been held on 22 June
2026.
 
The Mayor invited Councillor Begum to introduce
the report.
 
Councillor Begum introduced the report which set
out the year end position for revenue and capital for the financial
year 2025/26.  With regards to revenue
spend there was an increase in overspend since the reported period
10 position.  She explained that the
main reason for the increase had been due to the resources required
to support the Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).  Project team costs for work on LGR could not be
charged against capital budget. Provision had been made in the
2026/27 budget to cover these costs.
 
Councillor Begum added that the final year end
position also included £1.546 million capital Minimum Revenue
Position (MRP) which had resulted in an overall underspend against
the latest budget of £0.772 million.  She then referred to the capital spend, which was
set out in Appendix 3. 
 
Councillor Begum explained that the report had
been scrutinised by the Finance Scrutiny Committee at its meeting
on 22 June.  The recommendations had
been noted and there were no additional recommendations for Cabinet
to consider.  The scrutiny members had
shared some feedback that would be considered by her and the Chief
Finance Officer.  The feedback did not
have any impact on the report and its recommendations.  She welcomed any questions and Cabinet’s
support.
 
The Chief Finance Officer informed Cabinet that
the information before members would form part of the financial
statement, which had been published the day before in line with the
statutory deadline.  It would be audited
by the external auditor in September.
 
Councillor Pattinson noted the overspend within
the Housing and wellbeing department. 
This had been due to the external factors in the housing system,
which was mainly due to increased costs for temporary
accommodation.  The Housing team was
working to mitigate the risks and was using every piece of
legislation and strategy it could to reduce the numbers required to
be housed in temporary accommodation. 
This included the longevity of people staying there.  It predicted an overspend would continue but the
housing team would do everything it could to reduce the impact on
the council.
 
The
Mayor thanked the councillors for their comments and invited
Cabinet to vote on the recommendations in the report, including two
for referral to Council.
 
Resolved –
 

1.      that the 2025/26 revenue
year end position as summarised at section 4.1 of the report and
detailed in Appendix 1 has been considered and the outturn position
is noted.

 

2.      that the 2025/26 capital
year end position as summarised at section 4.3 of the report and
shown in detail in Appendix 2 has been considered.

 

3.     
that Cabinet recommends to Council the approval of the revised
capital investment programme of £43.566m for 2026/27,
£13.505m for 2027/28 and £3.492m for 2028/29, including
rephasing of £13.660m capital budgets from 2025/26 into
2026/27 onwards as set out in Appendix 2.

 

4.      that Cabinet recommends to
Council to delegate responsibility to the Portfolio Holder for
Finance, in consultation with the Chief Finance Officer, to
transfer any surplus arising from any changes in proposed capital
financing charges to reserves.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the year end Financial Monitoring Report for 2025/26, with a focus on overspend due to Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) project costs, and recommend approval of the revised capital investment programme for the upcoming years.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Associate Director of Customer and
Corporate Services, Delivery Support Lead, Intelligence,
Performance and Improvement Lead and Community Commissioning Lead,
which provided an update of the outcomes that had been achieved
over the final quarter of 2025/26.
 
The Mayor thanked officers for the amount of work
that went into this report.  He said
that Councillor Stotesbury had noted the progress on the Green
Loop.  This had been a commitment in the
2022 election.  The ongoing improvements
were welcomed, including the new crossing by Oxhey Activity Park
and B & Q.  There was also reference
to big projects including the refurbishment of Watford Central
Leisure Centre.  He acknowledged the
successful delivery of the 2026 elections that had been delivered
by the Elections Manager and her team. 
He also highlighted the tendering of the Outreach contract with New
Hope.  It highlighted the work the
council did with agencies to support vulnerable
people.
 
The Mayor invited Councillor Hill to
speak.
 
Councillor Hill said the first thing she had been
going to mention was the delivery of the 2026 local elections,
particularly as these were likely to be the last Mayoral and
Watford Borough elections to be held. 
She also noted the roll out of digital services, particularly the
integration of AI and customer services.  There had been reduced waiting times for
customers’ calls during Q4 as a result.  This was vital as it was a way many residents
interacted with the council.  She
thanked the Associate Director and the team for ensuring it all ran
smoothly. 
 
The Chief Executive said that members had already
highlighted key areas.  She added her
thanks to all staff who had worked hard to make it
happen.
 
As there were no further questions or comments,
the Mayor invited Cabinet to vote on the
recommendations.
 
Resolved –
 

1.     
that Cabinet notes the final updates within the report relating
to:
 

·    
The Council Plan 2022-26 and Delivery Plan 2024-26
(Appendix A)

·    
The external key performance indicator results for
Quarter 4 of 2025/26 (Appendix B)

·    
The Voluntary Sector Commissioning Framework metrics
for Quarter 4 of 2025/26 (Appendix C)

·    
The council’s key corporate strategies
(Appendix D)
 

2.      that Cabinet notes the
progress updates relating to the Delivery Plan, key performance
indicators and key corporate strategies will be presented to
Overview and Scrutiny Committee in July 2026.

 

3.      that the proposed
amendments to the key performance indicators for 2026/27 are
agreed.

purpose:
Demolition of existing building and erection
of a part one, part five, and part six-storey building comprising a
commercial unit on the ground floor (Use Class E) and 24 flats
above (Use Class C3).
content:
The
committee received a report of the Principal Planning Officer,
which set out details of the full planning permission
application.  It was noted that an
update sheet had been circulated which explained that a further
response had been received from HCC Highways, including proposed
conditions.  The HCC Highways statement
had concluded that the Section 106 obligation for Travel Plan
monitoring was not required.
 
The
Chair invited the Principal Planning Officer to introduce the
report.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer set out details of the location and the
current proposal.  The applicant had
worked with officers and the Design Review Panel on the
proposal.  At the end of the second
review meeting the panel had given positive comments.  The officer explained the view of the proposed
premises from Station Road and the rear of the
building.  The site was in a highly
accessible location.  There were no
larger units of three-bedrooms. 
However, it was not considered a suitable location for
families.  A viability appraisal had
been carried out and independently reviewed for the
council.  The developer was unable to
provide any affordable housing.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer then explained the impact of the
development on surrounding properties. 
There was a negative impact on 1 Westland Road, although the front
windows of the property were not impacted and the impact to the
amenity space was acceptable.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer informed members about the County
Highways objection and the servicing of the site.  However, conditions had been proposed in the
update sheet to resolve this.  Servicing
was possible from the front of the building within specific
times.  Officers had considered it would
be unreasonable to refuse it on the grounds of
servicing.  It was noted that servicing
from Verulam Passage would be difficult.  The application was recommended for approval
subject to the completion of a Section 106 agreement and the
conditions set out in the report and the update sheet.
 
The
Chair invited members to make comments about the application or put
questions to officers.
 
The
main focus of the discussion was about the servicing of the
building.  It was noted that Verulam
Passage was mainly used by pedestrians, although this seemed to be
the preference of the County Highways department.  The best solution needed to be considered and this
was felt to be from the front of the building.  It was recognised that Station Road was a busy
route, particularly during rush hour when it could be
congested.  There was some concern about
the impact of servicing on other users of this road.  Officers were asked for further clarity on the
comments from the County Highways department.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer advised the committee that the County
Council, was a statutory consultee.  Any
comments they provided were taken seriously.  They considered the application against their
policies.  This was different to the
approach taken by planning, where planning officers balanced the
benefits of the development against the negatives.  The National Planning Policy Framework indicated
it should only be refused if there was an impact on highway
safety.  In this case there was already
an existing commercial building which could be brought back into
use at any time.  There were loading
time restrictions on the road.  If these
restrictions were breached it would not be a planning
matter.  It was necessary to compare the
existing with the proposed development, balanced with a car free
development on a brownfield site in an accessible
location.
 
There
was still some concern about the day to day use of the site and
servicing requirements.  The officer
clarified the works that would be required by Highways.
 
Another
concern raised was whether the site was needed for residential use
and the council’s five-year supply.  The Associate Director of Planning and Development
confirmed the council was over its five-year supply
requirement.
 
Councillor Martins was concerned about the
development.  He felt that if there was
no pressure to meet the five-year supply, then the council should
not let the quality of developments drop.  He also asked for a further explanation about the
site not being suitable for families. 
 
The
Principal Planning Officer referred to the impact of daylight and
sunlight on some of the units.  The
information from the BRE was guidance. 
Some windows were below the guidance but it was not
significant.  With regards to the
question about family accommodation, the site was on a busy road in
a commercial area.  These areas were
less suited to family accommodation. 
During the design development phase a shared amenity space had been
considered, but it would have been dark.  This was a constrained site.  Each unit would have its own terrace or balcony,
which met the amenity space guidance.
 
Councillor Martins was still concerned about the development and
felt that it could be turned down as it did not comply fully with
planning.
 
Councillor Sharpe stressed the opportunities of Town Centre
sites, including being close to amenities, public facilities and
transport.  The downside was that they
may not comply with every policy.  It
was necessary to decide what was most important.  He said it was necessary to compare the derelict
building with a high quality development.  He considered the application should be
approved.
 
The
Chair thanked members for their comments.  He sympathised with Councillor Martins’
views, but recognised the comments made by Councillor
Sharpe.
 
The
Chair asked the committee to vote on the officer’s
recommendation to grant the application, subject to a section 106
agreement and the conditions as set out in the report and the
update sheet
 
On
being put to the committee, the application was
approved.
 
Resolved –
 
That
planning permission be granted subject to the following
conditions:
 

Section 106 Heads of Terms
 

a.         Viability
Review Mechanism

 

           
To secure a review mechanism of the viability of the development to
be undertaken. This shall allow a financial payment to be made
towards affordable housing provision where the viability of the
development can be shown to have improved to provide a financial
surplus. 

 

b.         Exclude
Parking Permit Eligibility for Occupants

 

           
To secure a financial payment to the Council of £2,000
towards the variation of the Borough of Watford (Watford Central
Area and West Watford Area) (Controlled Parking Zones)
(Consolidation) Order 2010 to exclude the site from the controlled
parking zone, thereby preventing residents’ parking permits
being issued to the future occupiers of this site.

 

1.         Time
Limit

 

           
The development to which this permission relates shall be begun
within a period of three years commencing on the date of this
permission.

 

2.         Approved
Drawings

 

           
The development hereby permitted shall be carried out in accordance
with the following approved drawings:

Pre-commencement

 

3.         Demolition
Management Plan

 

           
No development, including demolition, shall commence until a
Demolition Environmental Management Plan has been submitted to, and
approved in writing by, the Local Planning Authority.

 

           
The Demolition Management Plan must include details of:

 

a)        demolition vehicle
numbers, type, routing;

b)        access arrangements
to the site;

c)         traffic
management requirements;

d)        demolition and
storage compounds;

e)        siting and details
of wheel washing facilities;

f)         cleaning of
site entrances, site tracks and the adjacent public
highway

g)         timing of
demolition activities (including delivery times and removal of
waste) and to avoid busy times;

h)        where works cannot
be contained wholly within the site, a plan should be submitted
showing the site layout on the highway including extent of
hoarding, pedestrian routes and remaining road width for vehicle
movements;

 

4.         Construction
Management Plan

 

           
No development shall commence until a Construction Management Plan
has been submitted to and approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority. Thereafter the construction of the development shall
only be carried out in accordance with the approved
Plan:

 

           
The Construction Management Plan shall include details
of:

 

a.     
Construction vehicle numbers, type, routing;

b.     
Access arrangements to the site;

c.       Traffic management
requirements

d.     
Construction and storage compounds (including areas designated for
car parking, loading / unloading and turning areas);

e.       Siting and details
of wheel washing facilities;

f.       Cleaning of site
entrances, site tracks and the adjacent public highway;

g.       Timing of construction
activities (including delivery times and removal of waste) and to
avoid school pick up/drop off times;

h.     
Provision of sufficient on-site parking prior to commencement of
construction activities;

i.
       Post
construction restoration/reinstatement of the working areas and
temporary access to the public highway;

j.        where works cannot
be contained wholly within the site a plan should be submitted
showing the site layout on the highway including extent of
hoarding, pedestrian routes and remaining road width for vehicle
movements;

k.       Phasing Plan.

 

5.         Flood Risk
Assessment and Drainage Strategy

 

           
No development shall commence until a Flood Risk Assessment and
Drainage Strategy for the site, including the details referred to
in the Local Lead Flood Authority consultation response, has been
submitted to, and approved in writing by, the Local Planning
Authority. The development shall not be brought into use until the
strategy has been implemented in accordance with the approved
details.

 

6.         Interim and
Temporary Drainage Measures

 

           
No development shall commence until details and a Method Statement
for interim and temporary drainage measures during the demolition
and construction phases have been submitted to, and approved in
writing by, the Local Planning Authority.

 

           
Pre-specific part of development

 

7.         Detailed
Design

 

           
No development shall commence on the superstructure of the building
until detailed elevations (at scale 1:20), showing all the recessed
and projecting details (including stone banding, terraces,
balconies, balustrades, brick panels, ground floor frontage and
pipework) have been submitted to and approved in writing by the
Local Planning Authority. The development shall only be constructed
in the approved finish and materials.

 

8.         External
Materials

 

           
No external facing materials shall be installed on the building
until full details and samples of all external facing materials
(including reconstituted stone, brickwork, doors, gates, panels,
windows, balustrades, pipework) have been submitted to and approved
in writing by the Local Planning Authority. The development shall
only be constructed in the approved finish and
materials.
 
9.
       
Piling (Thames Water)
 

           
No piling shall take place until a Piling Method Statement
(detailing the depth and type of piling to be undertaken and the
methodology by which such piling will be carried out, including
measures to prevent and minimise the potential for damage to
subsurface sewerage infrastructure, and the programme for the
works) and piling layout plan including all Thames Water wastewater
assets, the local topography and clearance between the face of the
pile to the face of a pipe has been submitted to and approved in
writing by the local planning authority. Any piling must be
undertaken in accordance with the terms of the approved piling
method statement and piling layout plan.

 

           
Pre-occupation

 

10.     
Thames Water Condition 1

 

           
Prior to the first occupation or use of the development hereby
permitted confirmation shall be provided that either:

 

1.     
Foul water capacity exists off site to serve the development,
or

2.      A
development and infrastructure phasing plan has been agreed with
the Local Authority in consultation with Thames Water. Where a
development and infrastructure phasing plan is agreed, no
occupation shall take place other than in accordance with the
agreed development and infrastructure phasing plan, or

3.     
All foul water network upgrades required to accommodate the
additional flows from the development have been
completed.

 

11.     
Thames Water Condition 2

 

           
Prior to the first occupation or use of the development hereby
permitted confirmation shall been provided that either:

 

           
a. all sewage works upgrades required to accommodate the additional
flows from the development have been completed; or

           
b. a development and infrastructure phasing plan has been agreed
with the Local Authority in consultation with Thames Water to allow
development to be occupied.

 

           
Where a development and infrastructure phasing plan is agreed no
occupation shall take place other than in accordance with the
agreed development and infrastructure phasing plan.

 

12.     
Delivery and Servicing Plan

 

           
Prior to the first occupation or use of the respective elements of
the development hereby permitted, two Delivery and Servicing Plans
shall have been submitted to and approved in writing by the Local
Planning Authority covering the retail and residential elements
respectively. The D&SPs shall include details of the management
of deliveries to the site, arrangements for waste collection and
(for the residential D&SP) management arrangement for tenants
moving in and out of the site premises. Both D&SPs need to
reference how delivery and servicing will be co-ordinated between
the two different uses proposed for the site and include a strategy
for the timing of service vehicle movements and protocols for
arrival at the site.

 

13.     
Stopping up Existing Dropped Kerb

 

           
Prior to the first occupation or use of the development hereby
permitted, the existing vehicular access onto Station Road shall be
permanently stopped up and closed. The kerb and footway shall be
reinstated to the same levels and profile as the adjoining
footway.
 
14.
      Travel
Plan
 

           
At least 3 months prior to the first occupation / use of the
approved development a detailed Travel Plan Statement for the
commercial element of the site shall be submitted to and approved
in writing by the Local Planning Authority in consultation with the
Highways Authority. The approved Travel Plan Statement shall be
implemented in accordance with the timetable and target contained
in therein and shall continue to be implemented as long as any part
of the development is occupied subject to approved modifications
agreed by the Local Planning Authority in consultation with the
Highway Authority as part of the annual review.

 

15.     
Prior to the first occupation or use of the development hereby
permitted, full details of both hard and soft landscape works shall
have been submitted to, and approved in writing by, the Local
Planning Authority. These details must include:

 

a)     
paving;

b)     
bollards;

c)     
gravel;

d)     
pathways;

e)     
sedum roof;

f)       blue roof; and

g)      a
Landscape Management and Maintenance Plan.

 

           
The hard landscaping works shall be carried out in accordance with
the approved details prior to first occupation of the development.
The soft landscaping works shall be carried out in accordance with
the approved details not later than the first available planting
and seeding season after completion of development.
 

           
For observation
 

16.     
Provide Bike and Refuse Store

 

           
No residential dwelling shall be occupied until the Bike Store and
refuse store, as shown on drawing number 2415-PL08-F are made
available for use. These facilities shall be retained at all times
for the use by residents.

 

17.     
Water Efficiency

 

           
The residential dwellings hereby approved shall be completed to
meet the water efficiency requirement of 110 litres of water per
person per day.

 

18.     
Noise

 

           
No dwelling shall be first occupied until the recommendations of
the Environmental Noise Impact Assessment Report for Planning,
Report Reference 20958.ENIA.RPT.01, have been implemented and/or
undertaken in full.

 

19.     
Ground Floor Commercial Unit Use as Class E

 

           
The ground floor commercial unit shall be used for Use Class E
(Commercial, Business and Service) of the Schedule to the Town and
Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987.

 

20.     
Removal of Office to Residential Permitted Development
Rights

 

           
Notwithstanding the provisions of Article 3 of the Town and Country
Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) Order 2015 (as
amended) (or any modification or re-enactment thereof), no
development permitted under Schedule 2, Part 3, Class MA of the
Order shall be carried out without the prior written permission of
the Local Planning Authority.

 

21.     
Contamination

 

           
Any contamination that is found during the course of construction
of the development that was not previously identified shall be
reported immediately to the Local Planning Authority. Development
on the part of the site affected shall be suspended and a Risk
Assessment carried out and submitted to, and approved in writing
by, the Local Planning Authority. Where unacceptable risks are
found, remediation and verification schemes shall be submitted to,
and approved in writing by, the Local Planning Authority. These
approved schemes shall be carried out before the development is
resumed or continued.

 

22.     
Plant

 

           
Details of any new external plant or machinery shall be submitted
to and approved in writing by the Local Planning Authority. In
respect of any plant that emits sound, details shall include
appropriate noise assessments carried out in accordance with BS4142
and undertaken by appropriately qualified technical consultants.
The noise assessment shall include details of any necessary
mitigation, which shall be installed prior to the plant being
brought into operation.

 

23.      Highway Improvements
– offsite

 

           
A) Design Approval Notwithstanding the details indicated on the
submitted drawings, no on-site works above slab level shall
commence until a detailed scheme for the off
site highway improvement works has been submitted to and
approved in writing by the Local Planning Authority in consultation
with the Highway Authority. The works constitute: - the repaving of
the frontage of the site on Station Road; - measures to deter
footway parking; - removal of the redundant cross-over and; -
additional measures to support the dual use of this area as a
shared footway / cycleway.

 

           
B) Implementation / Construction Prior to the first use of the
development hereby permitted the improvement works referred to in
part A of this condition shall be completed in accordance with the
approved details.
topline: The Development Management Committee has decided to grant planning permission for a development project in a highly accessible location, despite concerns about servicing and impact on surrounding properties.

purpose:
Variation of condition 2 (approved drawings)
to increase the depth of house, introduce bay windows to front and
changes to the shape and position of the rear outbuilding.
Variation of condition 9 (arboricultural assessment) to account for
design changes pursuant to application 24/00977/FUL
content:
The
committee received a report of the Principal Planning Officer,
which set out details of the variation application.  It was noted that an update had been circulated
prior to the meeting which explained that additional details and
updated drawings had been submitted.
 
The
Chair began by noting that there was no speaker on behalf of the
applicant.  However, the applicant had
submitted a written statement which had been circulated to the
committee.  The statement would also be
added to the case file.  He explained
the procedure that would be followed and asked the committee to
confirm that they agreed that Councillor Duduta could speak on this
item.  The committee agreed.
 
The
Chair invited the Principal Planning Officer to introduce the
application.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer introduced the report.  He provided the committee with details of the
location of the property and design of the properties on the
estate.  He explained that the proposal
was an amendment to a previously consented application.  The amended application included three key
points:
 
1.
Increased proportion of the house
2.
Introduction of bay windows to the front of the property
3.
Changed shape and position of the outbuilding
 
The
Principal Planning Officer advised that with regards to the first
point there would not be a significant disruption to the street
scene.  The neighbour had said that
there was a dispute about the boundary line, but the officer
advised this was a civil matter and not planning.  He explained the changes to the rear of the
property and their proximity to the side boundaries.  He confirmed the proposal did project further to
the rear than the neighbours’ properties.  The front bays were in keeping with the character
of the area.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer then referred to the
outbuilding.  The latest proposal was to
move it away from the boundaries.  The
applicant had signed a unilateral undertaking preventing its use as
not incidental to the main house.  For
example, it could not be used as an independent
dwelling. 
 
The
Principal Planning Officer explained that the latest proposal did
not breach 45 degree line, which was
used to ensure there was sufficient light to the habitable rooms in
the neighbouring properties.  Following
amendments to the current scheme conditions 3, 5, 6 and 7 were no
longer required.  Conditions 8 and 9 had
been amended.  He finished by informing
the committee that the proposed amended scheme would not cause any
significant harm to the neighbours.  It
had been recommended for conditional approval.
 
The
Chair noted that there had been significant concern about the 20
feet building line and whether the proposal protruded beyond
this.  He asked if the Principal
Planning Officer could clarify what regards the committee should
have to this matter.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer displayed the plan which showed this
element of the scheme.  He explained
that the properties on this road were all broadly similar in
design, some with bay windows and some flat fronted.  The bay did come beyond the building line of one
neighbour’s front building line, but the main building line
was the same.  The other side did not
upset the building line.  Following a
further question from the Chair, he advised that if it was
noticeably beyond the building line this was a reason for
refusal.  Consideration was given from
the front wall and not the front of the bay window.
 
The
Chair then asked about the outbuilding and the concerns about the
damage that would be done to the tree roots in its
vicinity.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer replied that this matter had been
addressed in the updated conditions, one of which related to a tree
protection plan.  The proposal showed
that the outbuilding would be constructed using screw piles and not
trenches.  No tree protection order was
in place, but officers would not want the trees to be
damaged.
 
Councillor Hill asked for clarity about whether the depth of the
bay window should be considered.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer confirmed that officers considered the
main front wall and not the bay.
 
The
Chair invited Peter Jeffree to speak to the committee about the
proposal.
 
Mr
Jeffree advised that there were five concerns about the
proposal.  The first was that the
proposed house was significantly deeper and extended beyond the
front building line by one metre.  In
addition, it was set further back at the rear.  He referred to the Residential Design Guide and
the requirement for any new development to be in line with existing
building lines.  He also referred to the
Character of the Area Study, stressing the importance of the
character of the surrounding houses, which included a sense of
space.  The current proposal was
in close proximity to the neighbouring
properties and would block views to the trees beyond.  This would be contrary to the advice set out in
the Residential Design Guide.
 
Mr
Jeffree stated his second point related to how the proposal ignored
the local domestic character.  The
proposed building had a flat façade.  The roof was taller and bulkier than its
neighbours and was set further forward. 
It was felt this would give the building an over-bearing appearance
when viewed from the street.
 
The
third point Mr Jeffree raised was to the encroachment on the
boundary of the neighbouring property at 28.  The fence, owned by the resident at 28 had been
removed along the flank elevation.  He
recognised this was not a planning consideration but felt it called
into question whether the appropriate notices had been correctly
served when the application had been submitted.
 
Mr
Jeffree moved on to his fourth point, which related to overlooking
due to the two large rear windows on the second floor being moved
nearer the garden.  It was considered
this exacerbated the problems of overlooking that were already
there.  This reduced the
neighbour’s privacy and amenity.
 
Mr
Jeffree said the final point was about the damage to the tree roots
due to the proposed garden room.  The
trees formed an environmental barrier, screening the houses from
the noise and pollution from the college.  He finished by stating that it came to a point
when it was possible to say when ‘enough’ became
‘too much’.  He considered
this application had reached that point.  He urged the committee to reject the
application.
 
The
Chair thanked Peter Jeffree.  He asked
officers to clarify the comments about the loss of privacy that had
been raised.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer advised that from the front view it did
appear to be a two-storey dwelling consistent with Cassiobury
Drive.  He said that the windows at loft
level were equivalent to dormers in a two-storey house; they were
set in from the boundaries.  In
residential streets there was a mutual degree of
overlooking.  It would be difficult to
state that there was a loss of privacy to either side.  It would be no different to having dormer
windows.
 
The
Chair invited Councillor Duduta, a Park ward councillor to speak to
the committee.
 
Councillor Duduta explained he was speaking as a Park ward
councillor and on behalf the local
residents.  Residents recognised
the need to improve homes and modernise them.  However, their main concern was that replacement
houses were becoming larger and changing the character of the
area.  It was felt this application may
be larger than the original proposal. 
It had been noted that it was further forward than the neighbouring
property.  Although the officer had
advised that it was acceptable, residents had concerns about its
appearance.  They were also concerned
about the trees, which were important in screening the houses from
the college.  He appreciated that the
committee needed to consider the application based on planning
policies.  He wanted to ensure that
residents’ concerns had been put before the
committee.
 
The
Chair thanked Councillor Duduta for his presentation.  He said that he and the committee had been
impressed with the concerns raised by residents and would be
addressed during the committee’s discussions.  He invited comments and questions from the
committee.
 
In
response to a question from Councillor Saffery about the reference
to an arboricultural report and impact on the trees, the Principal
Planning Officer advised that the report referred to the screw
piles, which would not harm the trees. 
The report stated that they would be retained and there was no
reason to dispute it.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer responded to a question from Councillor
Martins.  He confirmed that the change
of character of an area was a material planning
consideration.  He explained that the
Cassiobury Estate was different to how it was in the
1950s.  It was not part of a
conservation area.  There were larger
houses on the estate.  The main factor
was consistency of the street scene. 
The proposal was in proportion with the character of Cassiobury
Estate as it was now. 
 
Councillor Sharpe referred to Peter Jeffree’s comment
about terracing effect.  There was a
broad impression that the typical style of Cassiobury Estate was
‘Metroland’ and did not have the standard double
fronted houses.  However, this was not
unknown in Cassiobury Drive.  He asked
officers for their comments about how far it was possible to insist
on retaining the typical style of the area.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer said that the designs on the Cassiobury
Estate did vary.  The policy asked for
buildings to be in character.  He
explained the typical character of the houses in
Cassiobury.  The proposal was broadly in
character with the description.  With
regards to the terracing effect, he explained the existing garage
was up to the boundary line.  There was
still some separation between the properties at the upper level
which was fundamental to the character.
 
Councillor Bell commented that he had been concerned about the
proposal following Peter Jeffree’s presentation.  However, having heard from the officer and seen
the photos it did not appear there was a dramatic
difference.  He acknowledged that this
was not in a conservation area.  Also,
he did not feel it sufficiently changed the character of the
area.  He did not feel there was enough
information to refuse the application. 
 
Councillor Hill noted that the resident had signed an agreement
that the garden room could not be used as a dwelling in the
future.  She understood that some
residents were still not happy about it.
 
Councillor Saffery stated that it was important to remember that
there was already an approved scheme for this site.  If the application was refused and went to the
Planning Inspectorate, this application was not that
different.  It was important to balance
all factors.
 
Councillor Sharpe said that the committee should take notice of
objections.  It was then necessary to
consider the information and what made it unacceptable.  This application was well set back from the road
and the design was not jarring or bulky.  He sympathised with residents, but the committee
needed to consider any grounds for refusal.  He felt it would be difficult to refuse this
application.
 
The
Chair commented that he had seen Cassiobury Estate change over the
years.  He sympathised with residents
and recalled discussions about another road on the
estate.  New properties reflected the
modern lifestyle.  If the previous
decision did not exist there could be a stronger case.  However, this application proposed marginal
changes.  He asked the committee to vote
on the officer’s recommendation to grant the application,
subject to conditions as set out in the report and the update
sheet.
 
On
being put to the committee the application was approved.
 
Resolved –
 
That
planning permission be granted subject to the following
conditions:
 
1.
       
Time Limit
 

           
The development to which this permission relates shall be begun
before 9th April 2028.  
 
2.
       
Approved Drawings
 

           
The development hereby permitted shall be carried out in accordance
with the following approved drawings:
 
           
424-200 Rev A
           
424-001 Rev C
           
424-202 Rev C
           
424-203 Rev A
           
424-204 Rev B
           
424-205 Rev D
           
424-206 Rev C
 

3.         The proposed
first floor side windows in the north-western and south eastern side elevations of the dwelling shall
be permanently fitted with obscure glass and the part of the window
less than 1.7m above internal floor level shall be permanently
fixed closed. 

 

4.         No part of the
development shall be occupied until details of renewable
technologies (such as Air Source Heat Pumps (ASHP) and PV Panels)
have been submitted to and approved by the Local Planning Authority
detailing the energy saving measures and renewable and low-energy
sources to be installed, as set out in principle in the Energy
Statement by Oakland Energy (24/11/2024) and drawing No. 424-003
Rev E. If the ASHP is to exceed the limitations of Schedule 2, Part
14, Class G of The Town and Country Planning (General Permitted
Development) (England) Order 2015 (as amended), a noise impact
assessment and any mitigation measures shall be included in the
details. The dwelling shall not be occupied until the works have
been carried out in accordance with the approved
details.

 

5.         The
development shall only be carried out in accordance with the tree
protection measures detailed in the Arboricultural Method Statement
and Tree Protection Plan by Arbol EuroConsulting Ref. 101954, 04/02/2026). No works,
including demolition, shall commence on-site until the Protective
Measures have been implemented and these measures shall be
maintained as such at all times whilst
the construction works take place. The development shall only be
carried out in accordance with the Main Construction Works outlined
on page 18 of the Arboricultural Method Statement.
 

6.         Prior to
commencement of works (including vegetation clearance), a suitably
qualified ecologist will inspect the site and surrounding area
(Badger Survey Report, AEWC Ltd, 24-163, February 2025) to check
for any new badger setts. If new setts or entrance holes are
present within 30m of the proposed works, appropriate mitigation to
safeguard them must be submitted to the Local Planning Authority
for approval, and a licence may be required from Natural
England.

 

7.         All of the
dwellings hereby approved shall be built to The Building
Regulations (2010) Access to and Use of Buildings, Approved
Document M (2015 as amended), Volume 1: Dwellings, M4(2):
Accessible and adaptable dwellings standard.

 

8.         Prior to
occupation the renewable technologies in the Renewable Technology
Statement (dated: 28th May 2026) shall be installed and brought
into use. 
 

9.        
Notwithstanding the provisions of Article 3, Schedule 2, Part 1 of
the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order
2015 (or any modification or reenactment thereof), no enlargements
of a dwelling house permitted under Classes A, AA, B and
E shall be carried out or constructed
without the prior written permission of the Local Planning
Authority.

 

10.     
No part of the flat roof of the development hereby permitted shall
be used as a terrace, balcony or other open amenity
space.
topline: The council has decided to approve a variation application for a property, despite concerns raised by local residents about the size and character of the proposed building.

purpose:
Erection of part single, part two-storey rear
extension, hip-to-gable loft conversion with rear dormer and
permeable driveway retrospective
content:
The
committee received a report of the Planning Officer, which set out
details of the householder planning permission
application.
 
The
Chair invited the Planning Officer to introduce the
report.
 
The
Planning Officer informed the committee of the location of the site
and style of property.  He advised that
there was hardstanding to the front of the property for two
vehicles and to the rear.  He provided a
comparison of the pre-existing building with the
application.  He noted that this was a
retrospective application to approve the existing
structure.  He advised that properties
with six-bedrooms and used as a house in multiple occupation did
not require planning permission. 
Highways had responded that they had no objections and there was no
harmful impact and an application had been made to the county
council for a dropped kerb.
 
The
Planning Officer informed the committee that some of the
development would be considered as permitted lawful
development.  Some did not meet the
design guidance but as it was permitted development it could not be
refused.    The application
had been submitted to summarise all of
the development.  With regards to visual
impact there was still separation between the properties as shown
in the photos.  The first floor extension was proportionate and modest
of the projection and therefore had no visual impact on the
neighbours.  The recommendation was to
approve the retrospective application.
 
The
Chair asked the officers to explain the process by which the
applicant had developed the property. 
 
The
Development Management Lead explained that the property benefitted
from previous development as set out in the history contained in
the report.  This included permitted
development and a Lawful Development Certificate for the loft
conversion.  The single storey rear
extension was permitted as a householder permitted development
scheme; this could be built on its own. 
There was permission for a first floor
extension.  Separately these could all
go ahead.  However, the applicant had
built them all in one phase.  This meant
that in accordance with legislation that as the first floor extension had been built with another
extension it was no longer considered to be permitted
development.  This has required the
various developments to require permission as one
proposal.  As part of the justification,
officers had taken into account that
each element could have been done under permitted
development.  This was a procedural
matter to combine all of the matters
into one.
 
The
Chair commented on the loft development.  There were no questions for officers from the
committee.  The Chair invited Jannice
Piantadosi to speak to the committee.
 
Mrs
Piantadosi informed the committee that she was the owner of the
adjacent property.  She would take it
that the committee had read her original objection.  She stated that the applicant had no respect for
the committee otherwise they would not have submitted a
retrospective application which was inaccurate.  She advised that although the report stated the
dormer was 0.23 metres from the party wall, this was incorrect as
it sat virtually on the party wall. 
This would affect her if she wished to build a loft conversion in
the future.  The report also mentioned
parking at the rear of the property, this was also incorrect as
there was no open access.  The parking
at the front consisted of rubble with a hedge all the way
across.  With regards to waste
management there was insufficient bins for the number of
residents.  She circulated photos to the
committee.
 
Mrs
Piantadosi stated that the owner had no consideration for the
neighbours.  There had been no contact
with her about the party wall agreement.  She had been advised she could go ahead herself,
but there was no guarantee she would get the money
back.  The building site was not secure
and had been witnessed by Councillor Williams.  In the application they had stated that the works
would be finished by the middle of February, but it was
not.  The applicant solely wanted to
develop a house in multiple occupation. 
She questioned whether Watford needed this type of
developer.  She finished by stating that
the applicant had built the dormer close to her
property.
 
The
Chair thanked Mrs Piantadosi.  He noted
that the applicant’s behaviour was not a material
consideration.  However, he was shocked
that the applicant had not spoken to her.  He also noted that how the building works were
conducted was not a material planning consideration.  It had been confirmed that there were six people
living there and the property had six bedrooms and three
kitchens.  He reiterated following the
change in law, planning permission was not required for its use as
a house in multiple occupation.  The
Chair asked officers to clarify the positioning of the dormer
following Mrs Piantadosi’s comments.  He also asked officers that they were certain the
plans showed what had been built.
 
The
Development Management Lead responded that officers were aware that
the development had already taken place, which was the reason the
application had been submitted. 
Officers had to go by the plans that had been provided by the
applicant.  They had submitted the
application to remedy the breach.  If
the plans were different to the development they had done, they
would remain in breach.  If it did not
resolve the planning breach there would be further investigation
work by the planning enforcement team. 
She appreciated the frustration for officers and
residents.  The existing enforcement
case remained open at this time.
 
The
Chair confirmed that the committee would review the application as
demonstrated in the plans received by officers.  He invited the committee to make comments or ask
questions about the application.
 
In
response to a question from Councillor Hill about Party Wall Act
agreements, the Development Management Lead said that officers
were not able to advise on these
agreements as they could not be taken into consideration under
planning matters.
 
Following the resident’s
comments about her rights for a loft conversion, Councillor A
Saffery asked if officers could confirm the situation.  The Development Management Lead said that she
would have exactly the same rights in
planning terms.  She would need to
consider the access and structure. 
Permitted development rights applied to every house.
 
Councillor G Saffery queried whether the committee was being
asked to consider an application with all the relevant facts in
front of them.  The application referred
to hardstanding, but this appeared to be rubble.  There was also the question of the accuracy of the
information they had.  He asked officers
if the committee could defer the application for further
information to be supplied.  He welcomed
other members’ views. 
 
Councillor Sharpe responded that he preferred not to defer
applications.  However, he would want to
know that the development the committee had given permission for
was the same as had been built.
 
The
Development Management Lead explained that the use as a single
dwelling house or six-bedroom house in multiple occupation was
interchangeable. As planning permission was not
required.  The hardstanding was a net
increase of one parking space, it was
believed this was available to be used. 
However, no parking was required as part of the assessment of the
application.
 
The
Development Management Lead confirmed that the committee could
defer the application to ask for more information.  She reminded members that the applicant could
appeal if the application was not determined within the specified
time.
 
The
Chair said that he sympathised with the sentiment.  He reminded members that if they did grant the
application, planning enforcement had the information on the agreed
plans. It was not definite that the plans did need any
modification.  He would prefer not to
defer the decision, but it was the committee’s
decision.  He asked the officers for
their thoughts.
 
The
Development Management Lead said that having heard the points
raised by the resident, she shared the concerns about the
application.  She had also heard the
comments from Councillors Saffery and Sharpe and agreed about a
deferral.
 
There
was a question about the length of the deferral and when it would
be reconsidered by the committee.  The
Development Management Lead said that she hoped it could be brought
to the next available committee. 
Officers would need to look into the
accuracy of the plans and the development on site.  This would be subject to the co-operation of the
applicant. 
 
It was
confirmed the next meeting was on 21 July.  The Development Management Lead said that officers
would aim for that date if they could.
 
In
response to a question from the Chair, the Development Management
Lead advised that if the applicant did not co-operate with
officers, a decision could still be made based on the
plans.  However, she wanted to make sure
that the committee had accurate information to make that
decision.  She stressed that members
should not pre-determine the decision before they had all the facts
to consider.
 
The
Chair asked the committee to vote on deferring the application to
enable officers to investigate the accuracy of the information in
the application.
 
On
being put to the committee, it was agreed the decision was deferred
to a future meeting.
 
Resolved –
 
That a
decision be deferred to a future meeting.

The
committee received a report of the Development Management Lead,
which set out details of the request to vary previous planning
decisions.
 
The
Chair invited the Development Management Lead to introduce the
report.
 
The
Development Management Lead explained to the committee the site
location of the variation application. 
She advised that there would be no physical changes to the
development.  The proposal was to change
23 of the units from intermediate ownership to affordable
rent.  This proposal had been supported
by the Housing Team.  It was recommended
for approval.
 
Councillor Bell commented that he would have preferred more
social rent properties in the development.  However, it was positive that the 23 intermediate
ownership units had been changed to affordable housing.
 
Councillor Hill said that it was good to see larger properties
being built.  The social housing was
needed.
 
In
response to a comment from Councillor Short about the state of the
road and it needing to be resurfaced, Councillor Bell who was also
the county councillor for the area said that the county council
would see what could be done.
 
The
Chair invited the committee to vote on the officer’s
recommendation as set out in the report.
 
On
being put to the committee, the variation application was
approved.
 
Resolved –
 
That
the request to vary the relevant Section 106 agreements of planning
permissions 18/00842/FULM, 22/01481/VARM and 25/00817/VAR be
approved and the agreement/s be varied as follows:
 

i)
         That the
23 dwellings defined for intermediate ownership be provided as
affordable rented tenure

ii)         All other
associated clauses and definitions be varied
accordingly.

content:
The
Chair invited the Director of Regeneration and Growth to present
the work programme to the committee.
 
The
Director of Regeneration and Growth informed the committee that the
draft work programme for the year ahead had been included for
members to review the content and suggest other potential
subjects.  An additional column had been
added, which would include specific questions or topics the
scrutiny committee would like covered. 
He advised that officers would therefore be asking members for more
information when topics were proposed. 
Some of the items on the draft programme had been included from the
long list members had suggested last year.
 
The
Director of Regeneration and Growth reminded members that the
council could not compel external organisations to attend a meeting
and take part in a scrutiny review. 
However, it was hoped that if they were asked they would make
themselves available.
 
The
Chair stated that the committee needed to look at services to
discover whether the council and other organisations were providing
value for money to Watford’s residents.  She invited members to put forward their ideas for
inclusion on the work programme.
 

AI and council technology
 
Councillor Osborn proposed that the committee should look at AI
usage, including the potential for the nuisance use of AI and the
submission of objections to planning applications.
 
The
Director reminded members that the committee had recently received
a presentation on the use of AI within the council.
 
It was
also suggested that the council could monitor AI’s carbon and
water impacts.  Another member referred
to the impact on jobs.
 

Chime Housing

 
There
was a discussion about inviting Chime Housing, formerly known as
Watford Community Housing and Thrive Housing prior to their
merger.
 
Councillor Kloss suggested it was necessary to identify specific
areas.  The Chair agreed and said she
would want it to be as a follow up to the previous
meeting.  She also felt that Anchor
Hanover should be invited to the meeting.
 

Emergency Housing Provision

 
Members
discussed reviewing emergency housing provision as the service was
under a lot of pressure.
 
Councillor Khan, who chaired Finance Scrutiny Committee, advised
that the Housing team reported into his committee.  They did not only discuss the financial aspects of
the service but ither areas as well.  As
the service was under pressure, he did not want to duplicate their
work and suggested that when the Housing team were next due to
attend Finance Scrutiny Committee, members from Overview and
Scrutiny could also be invited to attend.
 

Local Government Reorganisation (LGR)
 
It was
noted the LGR had been included in the work programme for
November.  There was a discussion
whether this was too soon and should be at a later
date.  It was suggested that if it was
reviewed in a year’s time then scrutiny could look at the
transition plans and impacts on services to residents.  However, it was felt that scrutiny needed to be on
top of LGR.  The Chair said that she
wanted scrutiny to be involved from the start in order for the
committee to shape the way forward.
 
The
Director of Regeneration and Growth acknowledged members’
comments.  The government’s
decision was expected in July.  He felt
it would be possible to have a discussion about the journey the
council would go through.
 
It was
suggested that a review of LGR could take place every six months,
which the Chair agreed.
 

Community Safety

 
Councillor Kloss noted that Community Safety had not been
included in the work programme.  This
was a subject the committee looked at annually.
 
The
Chair said that she would ensure this was included.
 
Resolved –
 
that
the scrutiny committee’s comments are noted and the programme
to be further developed.
topline: The Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to review various topics including AI, housing provision, and community safety.

car parking area and hardstanding, and erection of two buildings,
