content:
The
committee received a report of the Principal Planning Officer,
which set out details of the major application.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer provided extensive details of the
proposal submitted by the applicant, the location of the site and
referred to previous applications.  The
recommendation was to refuse the application for the reasons set
out in the report, which the officer explained in detail to the
committee.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer informed the committee that the
application before the committee proposed a loss of 90% of office
floorspace on this site.  The
council’s Local Plan resisted the loss of office space unless
there was clear marketing evidence to show it could not be
let.  In addition, the Local Plan
safeguarded commercial space on Clarendon Road.  The proposal did not safeguard the character of
the existing, which was a large office building.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer explained that the application and its
design had been reviewed by the Place Shaping Panel.  The report was attached as an appendix to the
report.  The comments had included that
the tower appeared to be much larger than the one at Clarendon
Works and was inelegant and bulky.  He
commented that the principle of tall buildings on Clarendon Road
was not unacceptable.  The proposed
application had a poor public realm. 
Clarendon Works had incorporated the parking into the
basement.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer then referred to the visual impact on
nearby heritage areas.  The application
would be visible from two conservation areas.  The first was the Civic Core, particularly by the
Pond.  The impact on this area
was considered to be less than
substantial harm.  Any harm needed to be
outweighed by public benefit.  The
applicant had not shown the application would have any public
benefit.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer referred to the Affordable Housing
requirement of 35%, which was set out in the Local
Plan.  The application proposed 8% or
9%, all of which were shared ownership. 
There was no social housing to be provided.  There was no independent review of viability and
therefore it was unacceptable. 
 
The
Principal Planning Officer moved on to the sunlight and daylight
assessment.  He informed the committee
that the assessment provided by the applicant had been done on
different plans to those included in the application.  It was considered that the degree to which the
proposal did not meet the guidance was severe.  He showed members an assessment that had been done
on one floor of the proposed building. 
Many of the units have poor sunlight and daylight to
them.  This was beyond the flexible
approach of the National Planning Policy Framework
(NPPF).  Daylight to the middle of the
site was very poor.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer then turned the committee’s
attention to the impact on properties in Monmouth Road, which was
to the north of the site.  The applicant
had not indicated the potential loss of light to these
properties.  The tower would be visually
overpowering and therefore the development was considered to cause
harm to the residential properties in Monmouth Road.  However, it was unlikely to have an impact on
Clarendon Works.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer stated that the presentation focussed on
the main issues, with details set out in the report.  The recommendation was to refuse the application
for the reasons set out in section nine.
 
The
Chair then invited Brigid Taylor to speak to the committee about
the proposal.
 
Ms
Taylor informed the committee that the application was proposed on
a highly sustainable underused site. 
The application proposed the inclusion of 24 affordable
homes.  She said that the reasons for
refusal, particularly loss of office space and design did not align
with the evidence.  She explained that
the net loss of office space was acceptable if evidence could show
that it was not required.  The existing
building had been empty since 2023 and
had been marketed for five years.  It
was unlettable.  There was a fundamental
shift in the need for office space.  The
council’s insistence on the requirement for office space was
not realistic.  The proposed application
had a commercial frontage and would bring vitality into Clarendon
Road.
 
Ms
Taylor then referred to the site.  It
backed on to Beechen Grove which was a gateway to the
town.  It mirrored Clarendon Works,
which currently looked isolated.  It was
an intelligently designed.  88% of the
residential units would have a dual aspect.  100% of the units had amenity space, either with a
balcony or outdoor space.  There were
three areas of shared amenity space. 
The application aligned with the Government’s push for new
housing on brownfield sites.  The net
loss of office space was justified.   The site would be car light, as it was close
to people’s place of work and transport.  The application provided 280 homes, which included
three-bedroom units and affordable housing.
 
The
Chair thanked Brigid Taylor.  He asked
officers to clarify the comments about the office space and the
reference to a document from 2024 which stated additional office
space was not required.  The second
clarification required, related to applicant’s statement that
the daylight aligned with requirements for brownfield standards
that the government considered acceptable.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer turned to the first point the Chair had
requested.  The South West Herts Economic Study was referenced in
the report.  It considered office use in
the vicinity of Clarendon Road.  The
report informed the committee that there had been lots of
developments in Clarendon Road.  The
study did not state there should be a loss of office
space.  It was about preserving the
office space.  The assumption that it
could be lost was not in the economic study.  With regard to the
question about brownfield sites.  He
agreed that this site did have the potential to be redeveloped,
including a taller building.  The
efficient use of the site would be welcomed.  He said that an application on this site could
re-provide office space as well as residential, similar to Clarendon Works adjacent.  However, the design of the proposal and the other
matters detailed in the report were unacceptable.
 
The
Chair asked for clarity on the loss of daylight to units, which the
applicant said was acceptable.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer explained that the NPPF did state that
in an urban environment it could be more difficult to meet the
requirements of daylight and sunlight in the BRE
guidance.  It had been discussed
previously at committee.  However, this
design with the enclosed courtyard created an issue that was not
there before.  The applicant had
referred to an appeal in their submission.  The particular site
that had been referenced, and its location, was different to the
proposal before the committee.  He
referred back to the presentation and
the plan which showed the amount of sunlight and daylight each unit
could expect.  He noted that this was a
typical example, but it would be worse on lower floors.  Some units were affected very badly.
 
The
Chair opened the discussion and invited comments from the
committee.
 
The
committee spoke about the differing views about the application and
how it was possible to imagine that officers and the applicant were
talking about two different buildings. 
The report was well evidenced.
 
In
response to a question about the possibility of converting the
existing building, the Principal Planning Officer advised that the
building was not very old.  However, it
would possibly be difficult to convert it to residential use;
although residential could perhaps be located to the
rear.  He said that there were a lot of
options that had not been explored. 
Members felt the question was whether the building could be
let.  There was also a question about
whether enough work had been done to consider the viability of the
site.  The officer advised that no
evidence had been provided that the building could not be
re-let.
 
The
members welcomed the detailed and well-argued report.  They were concerned about the large loss of office
space as a result of this
proposal.  There was also concern about
the impact on the residents of Monmouth Road.  One councillor commented that if the building
design was better, it would be more difficult to argue against the
officer’s recommendation.
 
Following a question from the Chair about residents’
feedback, the Principal Planning Officer advised that the NPPF
encouraged pre-application discussions. 
The applicant had sought officers’ views which had been
provided, including the loss of office space.  There were substantive flaws in the design which
had been raised with the applicant.  The
application had not been amended following the officers’
views being given.
 
The
committee also spoke of the low level of affordable housing offered
as part of this scheme.  Affordable
housing was a priority for the council. 
This scheme offered 24 shared ownership units.  This was well below the expected
level.  There was no justification for
the deviation from policy.  Clarendon
Works showed what could be achieved in this area.  It was important that schemes including housing
had a mix of unit sizes and not just small ones.
 
Members
welcomed the introduction of mixed-use schemes.  It was noted the Local Plan encouraged development
and did not prevent it.  Officers were
recommending upholding the Local Plan. 
The Local Plan had been designed to ensure the development of
successful schemes.  The reference from
the Place Shaping Panel was mentioned again and the comparison with
Clarendon Works.  The applicant needed
to take away the comments and to come back with a design that met
the council’s requirements.
 
The
Chair thanked the committee for their comments and proceeded to sum
up the discussion.  The Chair said that
the main issues were the loss of office space, the poor design, the
predominant residential appearance facing on to Clarendon Road, the
quality of the residential accommodation, particularly the low
levels of sunlight and daylight for some of the units, plus the
affordable housing offer, which was well below the policy
requirement.  He provided detail for
each of the reasons. 
 
The
Chair noted the proposal would result in a loss of 90% of office
floorspace.  The site was situated in
Clarendon Road, a primary office location.  It was a strategically important employment area
as identified in the Local Plan.  The
proposal did not protect the commercial role or character of the
road.  The applicant had not
demonstrated that the site was not suitable for office
use. 
 
The
Chair then spoke of the design of the site.  There was a failure to transition from the
two-storey buildings on Monmouth Road and would therefore appear
visually over-bearing.  The frontage on
to Clarendon Road would appear predominantly residential,
undermining the commercial character of the road.  The internal courtyard was enclosed and dominated
by car parking and limited natural surveillance.  There was little
community space and no play area for children.
 
With regard to the quality of the residential accommodation, this was judged to
be poor.  Some units had low lux levels,
some as low as 14-34 compared to the recommended 150 in the BRE
guidance.  The affordable housing offer
of 24 shared ownership units, equating to 8%, was far below the 35%
set out in the policy.  It was noted
that the applicant had failed to fund the independent viability
review that would be required to justify any shortfall.
 
Finally, the Chair noted that there were unresolved issues which
related to waste services and highways safety.  He felt the applicant had failed to fully engage
with officers the Place Shaping Panel and take on board comments
raised.  Overall, the scheme failed to
demonstrate that the benefits of the application outweighed the
concerns.
 
The
Chair asked the committee to vote on the officer’s
recommendation to refuse the application for the reasons set out in
the report.
 
On
being put to the committee the application was unanimously
refused.
 
Resolved –
 
That
planning permission be refused for the following
reasons:
 

1.         The proposed
development would result in a significant loss of office floor
space within Watford’s primary office area. Such a loss fails
to protect employment floorspace, fail to support economic growth
and detracts inward Investment to Watford which is contrary to paragraphs 85, 86 and
87 of the National Planning Policy Framework (2024) and Policies
SS1.1, CDA2.1, EM4.1, EM4.3 of the Watford Local Plan
2021-2038. 

 

2.         The proposed
development, by virtue of its height, massing, layout and facades
is considered to be of poor design. The
building would be visually harmful, failing to demonstrate
townscape rationale or a sense of place making and failing to
respond positively to the context or transition to lower lying
surroundings. The development does not offer townscape
justification, outstanding design or public benefits required to
outweigh the tall building impacts. The predominantly residential
appearance on Clarendon Road fails to safeguard the commercial role
and character of the area. The public realm lacks natural
surveillance being surrounded by inactive facades, is enclosed and
would be overshadowed and is dominated by car parking and hard
landscaping. The poor design quality of development and harm of the
development would be contrary to paragraphs 131, 135, 137, 139, of
the National Planning Policy Framework (2024) and Policies SS1.1,
CDA2.1, QD6.1, QD6.2, QD6.3, QD6.4, QD6.5, HE7.1 and HE7.2 of the
Watford Local Plan 2021-2038.
 

3.         The dominant
nature of the proposed development, in terms of its height, scale
and architectural design, would cause less than substantial harm to
the setting and significance of the Civic Core Conservation Area.
The harm is would not be outweighed by the public benefits of the
scheme and would be contrary to paragraphs 212 and 215 of the NPPF
and policies and QD6.5, HE7.1 and HE7.2 of the Watford Local Plan
2021-2038.

 

 

4.        
Notwithstanding the lack of qualified justification, the proposed
quality of accommodation, by virtue of the low levels of daylight
and sunlight to flats, the poor quality shared amenity areas with
no play or informal recreation space and the lack of generosity to
internal and external shared spaces are considered to create poor
quality living conditions which are contrary to paragraphs 131,
135, 137, 139 of the National Planning Policy Framework (2024) and
Policies SS1.1, HO3.11, CDA2.1, QD6.1, QD6.2, QD6.3, QD6.4 and
QD6.5 of the Watford Local Plan 2021-2038.
 

5.         Without the
ability to independently review the affordable housing provision,
the offer of 23 or 24 shared ownership flats is considered to fail
to meet identified housing needs contrary to paragraph 66 of the
National Planning Policy Framework (2024) and Policy HO3.3 of the
Watford Local Plan 2021-2038.
 

6.         The lack of
suitable waste storage capacity, without any clear plan of how this
be managed is contrary to paragraph 135 of the National Planning
Policy Framework (2024) and Policy QD6.4 of the Watford Local Plan
2021-2038.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Chief Executive, which contained the
Council Plan and Delivery Plan 2026-2028.  The plans would be forwarded to Council for final
approval.
 
The Mayor thanked officers for their work in
producing the Council Plan, which was based on his mayoral
manifesto, so quickly after the election.  He noted that some councils were still waiting to
approve their Council Leaders.  He,
therefore, felt that to have a Council Plan already was
impressive.
 
The Mayor stated that he wished to recognise the
previous plan and that vast proportion of the commitments had been
implemented.  The new Council Plan
contained many good commitments for Watford and everyone recognised
the restricted timeframe due to Local Government
Reorganisation.  He highlighted page 21
of the agenda pack and the commitment to better sports facilities
and accessible playgrounds.  He added
that safety was an important issue, including expanding
CCTV.  There was a commitment not to
increase Council Tax by more than the rate of
inflation.  It was proposed to increase
the number of green flag parks in the Borough and to plant more
trees.  The improvement to the energy
efficiency of buildings, including Watford Central Leisure
Centre.  He added the reference to a
Herts Film Festival based in Watford.
 
The Mayor asked that a change was made on page 27
of the report.  The reference was that
the council would ‘investigate hosting an ice
rink’.  He said that instead he
would like it to read ‘host an ice rink’ and not to
investigate, as he was aware that work was already
ongoing.
 
The Mayor invited Councillor Williams to
speak.
 
Councillor Williams
also wanted to give his thanks to officers for their work in
pulling the document together so quickly.  He noted the Mayor had already mentioned some of
the commitments he was going to raise. 
He said that members knew how much residents valued the
town’s parks and open spaces.   It was great to see this in the new Council
Plan and the greater commitment, including the increase in green
flags.  It was proposed to install water
fountains and improve the footpaths in local parks.  The council would support greater biodiversity
throughout the town.  The water quality
of rivers running through the town would be improved, for example
by the River Colne project.   As
the Mayor had mentioned about reducing carbon footprint of the
leisure centres, this had already been carried out at Woodside and
Central would be next.  He informed
members that a new additional Environmental Crime Officer would be
starting shortly.  Their role would
include tackling littering, dog fouling, fly tipping and increasing
the number of fixed penalty notices issued.  He noted that Watford was the lead authority in
Hertfordshire in issuing penalty notices and Watford continued to
issue them to show that the council would not tolerate these
incidents.  The council would continue
to work with Veolia to ensure waste was collected and disposed of
properly.  The council would continue to
provide top rated services for the next 22 months and deliver the
Mayoral commitments set out in the report.  His final comment was about the padel courts which
were now available and was an exciting investment for the
town.
 
The
Mayor referred to Councillor Williams’ comments about the
additional Environmental Crime Officer post and that good progress
had been made since it was passed in the budget.  He invited Councillor Dychton to speak.
 
Councillor Dychton said that she would firstly like to reflect
on the previous plan.  Despite financial
pressures and increasing demand for services, the council had
continued to deliver for residents.  The
council had supported people through the cost of living crisis,
strengthened the Community Safety Partnership and maintained
support for vulnerable people. She stressed that the achievements
had only been possible through strong collaboration between the
council, partners, voluntary organisations and the local
community.  She wished to thank everyone
for their hard work. 
 
Councillor Dychton said the 2026-2028 plan set out an ambitious
programme for the next 2 years.  Her
focus remained for a healthier, safer and more inclusive
Watford.  She highlighted some of the
relevant commitments, including the wellbeing of young people and
children, major events to bring the town together, and the delivery
of new facilities including the Museum of Watford.  Keeping residents safer remained a key
priority.  The council would strengthen
its work on violence against women and girls, working with the
Police and partners to keep everyone safe.  The core theme for the plan was
inclusion.  She was excited for the
initiatives to enhance the town, which presented opportunities and
challenges.
 
The
Mayor thanked the councillors for their comments and invited
Cabinet to vote on the recommendation in the report.
 
Resolved –
 
that
the proposed Council and Delivery Plans are approved for
progression to Council for a decision.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Council Plan and Delivery Plan 2026-2028 for Watford, focusing on improving services and facilities for the community.

purpose:
Report is for noting that Watford Borough
Council will secure and monitor Employment Skills and Social Value
benefits for Watford’s communities, from 1st June 2026 as a
year 1 pilot.
content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Economic Development Lead and Planning
Policy Officer, which provided an update on the Employment, Skills
and Social Value Service, details of the operational and funding
model and confirmation that the service was ready to launch as a
Year 1 pilot from 1 June 2026.
 
The Mayor noted that this fell within his
portfolio.  He thanked the officers,
including the Economic Development Lead for bringing the report
forward.  Members were aware that
developments in the town could be controversial.  This proposal ensured that developers brought
forward benefits to Watford residents. 
The report included the 10 priorities across employment, skills and
wider social value.  It was important
the framework was in place to ensure it was clear what the council
was asking.  Herts Futures would monitor
progress ensuring the service was delivered to benefit the
community.
 
The Director of Regeneration and Growth added
that in addition to applying to new developments in the town, it
would also apply to the council’s own procurement of
services, ensuring local value to the community. 
 
Councillor Pattinson welcomed the report and said
that it would be good for it to be applied to local registered
social housing providers, including newly merged Chime
Housing.  The organisation was one of
the area’s major employers.  She
felt the framework would be helpful for them.
 
The Mayor agreed and said that it was important
the principles were embedded in as many places as
possible.  He asked the Director of
Regeneration and Growth to respond to the comments about housing
providers. 
 
The Director of Regeneration and Growth advised
that in addition to this, there was also the Watford Business
Pledge.  This was a good opportunity for
other organisations, not just Hertfordshire local authorities, to
make that commitment to do the right thing when procuring services
and delivering social value for their
communities.
 
The Mayor commented that he was aware Everyone
Active now used a local cleaning firm. 
There were practical and tangible things coming out of the business
pledge work.
           
As there were no further question or comments,
the Mayor reiterated his thanks to officers and invited Cabinet to
vote on the recommendations.
 
Resolved –
 
That it
is noted Watford Borough Council will secure and monitor Employment
Skills and Social Value benefits for Watford’s communities,
from 1 June 2026 as a year 1 pilot.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to launch the Employment, Skills and Social Value Service as a Year 1 pilot in Watford, ensuring benefits for the community.

quality services and sustainable support of residents.  The continual review ensured the management of
risks at an early stage.  She thanked

the risks.  The risk register was a

She highlighted some of the key risks.

risk.  There were impacts through

led to rising costs and affect on

compliance had been closed as accreditation had been obtained by
all officers.  She recommended the

purpose: Annual review of RIPA Policy
content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Associate Director of Customer and
Corporate Services, which set out the annual update of the
policy.
 
The
Mayor invited Councillor Hill to introduce the report.
 
Councillor Hill introduced the updated policy.    She explained that local authorities
had access to data when investigating offences.  Officers were required to comply with the
Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.  The council had not used these powers for several
years.  However, the council was
required to review the policy and procedures annually.  There were some minor changes to reflect staffing
updates, otherwise the policy remained unchanged.  If agreed by Cabinet, the report would go forward
to Audit Committee for approval.
 
Councillor Pattinson noted that the policy had not been used for
a long time.  However, she noted that
there had been changes to enforcement following the introduction of
the Renters Reform Act.  She asked
whether there would be any training for officers to ensure they
complied with this policy.
 
Councillor Hill confirmed that training would be given and it
would be checked that the Renters Rights Act would be
incorporated.
 
The
Mayor noted there were no further comments or questions and invited
members to vote on the recommendation within the report.
 
Resolved –
 
That
the updated policy is recommended to Audit Committee for
approval.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve an updated policy on the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.

content:
The Mayor had
agreed that the Chief Executive could bring forward a late urgent
report to Cabinet.  The report sought
approval of the council’s proposed representations to the
Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) in
relation to the Structural Changes Order for Hertfordshire under
Local Government Reorganisation.
 
The Mayor invited the Chief Executive to present
the report, which had been circulated earlier to all Cabinet
members.
 
The Chief Executive said that all members were
aware of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).  At this point in time MHCLG were still of the view
that the Hertfordshire authorities would receive a decision before
parliamentary recess.   All 11
councils in Hertfordshire were invited by MHCLG to give their views
in writing on the Structural Changes Order.  This was the legal mechanism that set out how the
government would implement the change. 
It would set out the new structure, the dissolution of existing
councils, and the governance and transition arrangements in the
intervening period.  This would include
joint committees, shadow authority arrangements from 2027 and
framework for the first election.  The
Chief Executive stressed it was an important piece of
legislation.  It was important to ensure
that Watford was represented in the discussions with
MHCLG.  The information that was set
into the Structural Changes Order rested with the
Minister.  However, the council was able
to forward its submission. 
 
The Chief Executive advised that the report set
out the position as it currently stood. 
It was intended that the Hertfordshire Leaders’ Group would
discuss this at the next meeting on 10 June.  It was hoped that there would be collective
agreement about the approach to be taken.  Three different models would be presented in terms
of the Structural Changes Order, covering each of the three options
that were submitted to MHCLG.  Cabinet
was being asked to endorse the strategic position and to delegate
to her and the Elected Mayor to finalise the council’s
position, following the Hertfordshire Leaders’
Group.  It was important that Watford
had a clear and credible voice.
 
Councillor Williams thanked the Chief Executive
for bringing the report to Cabinet.  He
asked how the other Hertfordshire authorities were managing this,
for example were they able to take it to a Cabinet
meeting.
 
The Chief Executive responded that there would
probably be a mixed approach across the county.  She had discussed it with the Mayor and it was
felt right to bring it to Cabinet, allow members to have a view and
to agree the delegation.
 
The Mayor thanked Councillor Williams for his
questions and commented that he thought it was important to be as
transparent as possible.  He invited
Cabinet to vote on the recommendations.
 
Resolved –
           

1.         that
Cabinet notes the current position as set out in the
report.

 

2.         that
delegated authority be granted to the Elected Mayor and Chief
Executive, to finalise and submit the council’s position, in
relation to all matters pertaining to the Structural Changes Order
as outlined in this report.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations for the council's representations to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government regarding the Structural Changes Order for Hertfordshire.

Variation of condition 2. (approved plans) and
condition 9 (offsite highways improvements to amend fire strategy
and introduce second stair core to residential tower with
associated layout and elevational changes) of planning permissions
22/00484/FULM and 23/01101/VARM.
content:
The
committee received a report of the Principal Planning Officer,
which set out details of the application.  It was noted that no objections had been received
in relation to the variation application.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer introduced the report, providing details
of the location site and the proposed variation application,
setting out the differences with the approved scheme.  He advised that there was no change to the impact
on the neighbouring conservation area. 
The main changes were to internal reconfigurations and a slenderer
tower.  He noted that the county
council’s Highways Authority had objected to the proposal,
but this objection could be addressed by the amended
condition.  The Highways Authority had
not expanded on their comments.  The
Highways Authority had also commented on condition 9, off-site
highway works.  However, the applicant
was only proposing a change to refer to the amended plans. The
objections could not be justified as reasons to refuse the
variation application. 
 
The
Chair asked the officer to comment on the original scheme which had
been refused by the committee and then approved by the Planning
Inspector. 
 
The
Principal Planning Officer explained that the original scheme had
been refused for a number of reasons, including harm to the
conservation area, the quality of the accommodation and issues
relating to daylight and sunlight in some of the units.
 
Councillor Martins noted the reference that the flats would be
to rent rather than to buy and questioned why this would make it a
material consideration for the committee.   Members should be concerned about the
standard of living regardless of whether the units would be for
rent or sale.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer advised that the Planning Inspector had
given their opinion due to there being other amenity space and
break out areas available to residents. 
The Planning Inspector had concluded the standard of accommodation
was high.  The council was tied by the
Planning Inspector’s decision on the original
scheme.
 
In
response to a question from Councillor Martins about the weight
given to the Highway Authority’s comments, the officer
explained that it was felt the application should not be rejected
on a minor point that could be dealt with by condition.  He added that planning officers looked at the
whole of the development and not one specific area.
 
The
Chair noted that the Highway Authority had not given a technical
reason to refuse the application.
 
Councillor Bashir then referred to the BRE guidance and asked
how the two applications compared with the number of units falling
below the guidance.  The officer advised
that it was difficult to answer as the assessment was very
technical.  A significant number of the
original habitable rooms would have been below the suggested
standard, possibly a third.  The
variation application included a few more.  It was not a significant increase to the original
scheme. 
 
In
response to a further question about the BRE guidance, the officer
explained that the guidance was not policy.  It was typical that not all rooms in flats would
meet the guidance.  Due to the slimmed
down tower, there were more flats moved to a lower level, which
made it harder to meet the levels in the guidance.
 
The
Chair noted the comments and said that other applications had been
approved where some rooms did not have adequate light
levels.  It was also necessary to take
note of the Planning Inspector’s decision and
comments.  It would be difficult to
object on this ground.
 
The
Chair invited Mr Bennett to speak to the committee about the
proposal.
 
Mr
Bennett informed the committee that the site had been empty for the
last four years.  The site had been
abandoned; it was used as a dumping ground and anti-social
behaviour took place there.  The council
and residents had asked for the site to be boarded up and made
secure.  He compared it to other
building sites in Watford which had considered local
residents.  The owners had not spent any
money on the site’s security.  It
had been the Police and council that had arranged for the siren
alarm, which was a cost to residents. 
He felt that the owners had not shown any regard for the
residents.  The state of the site had an
impact on residents, who were unable to sell their
properties.  He questioned how much
longer the community would have to put up with the
eyesore.  It had been suggested that the
council should board up the site, engage security and then bill the
owner for the costs.
 
Mr
Bennett said that this was an important site in Clarendon
Road.  He noted that the Planning
Inspector had granted the application and questioned whether the
permitted time had run out. 
 
The
Chair thanked Mr Bennett and invited Councillor Dychton to
speak.
 
Councillor Dychton stated that she was present to speak against
the application again.  The proposed
variation was worse than the one that already been
approved.  It was demonstrably worse how
people would live there in accordance with National Planning Policy
Guidance 2025.  The building was located
at a prominent gateway site and a primary office
location.  It was located in a position
where a high quality exemplary development should be
delivered.  Standards should not be
allowed to slip.  She was not
challenging the principle of development, which had been
established through the 2023 appeal. 
However, the proposed variation provided was narrower but
important.  She questioned whether the
proposal made the quality of living better or worse.  She said the officer’s report was clear that
a greater number of rooms failed the BRE guidance.  The size of the courtyard had been
reduced.  Due to the building’s
location on Clarendon Road the level of light mattered.  She referred to the National Planning Policy that
required a high standard of amenities for future occupiers,
especially in Town Centre locations.
 
Councillor Dychton asked members to remember that Clarendon Road
was a key commercial corridor and was a flagship regeneration
area.  This site should meet high
standards and be a benchmark for future developments.  However, it was the opposite.  It increased the mass of office accommodation,
reduced the courtyard and more residents would lack
daylight.  In this case the optimisation
of the site had gone too far.  She
further referred to the National Planning Policy Framework,
particularly that applications should be refused for designs that
failed to improve quality.  The
committee needed to consider whether the negatives outweighed the
benefits of the scheme.  The benefits of
redeveloping and regenerating this site had been secured through
the extant permission.  In this case
members were being asked to accept an application that was worse
than the original.  She stressed that
the quality should be exemplary and therefore this application
should be refused.
 
The
Chair thanked Councillor Dychton.  He
noted that the comments about the loss of light had been covered
earlier.  He referred to Councillor
Dychton’s comment about optimising the site and asked the
officer for his comments.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer confirmed that reference was always made
in planning when considering high density developments,
particularly in core development areas such as this
location.  In this case the number of
flats and office floorspace remained the same.   It was neither more intense nor less intense
than the original scheme.
 
The
Chair thanked the officer and opened the meeting up to
members’ questions and comments.
 
Councillor Sharpe stated that if he were a Central Ward
councillor he would also be advocating the same concerns as those
raised.  Residents had also suffered
from the poor management of the site. 
He then explained that the committee’s role was to focus on
the precise planning merits of the application, taking into account
the National Planning Policy Framework and the Local
Plan.  In this case it was necessary to
consider the application in the wider context.  The main factor here was the appeal
decision.  It was not possible to refuse
the application as it had not met the BRE guidance.  It would be necessary to demonstrate that the
proposed change was so significant compared to the agreed
plans.  The Planning Inspector had been
clear in their assessment that it could not be expected to meet the
standards in a Town Centre location. 
The officer had already indicated that the Highway
Authority’s comment would not impress the Inspector and that
it could be managed through condition. 
He considered that the variation application was not that different
from the original scheme and that it would be difficult if it were
refused and then appealed. 
 
Councillor Martins did not agree with previous
comments.  He acknowledged that the
Inspector overturned the committee’s previous
decision.  However, the proposed
variation was markedly different.  The
officer had acknowledged that more residents would be adversely
affected.  He felt that if the Inspector
was presented with this proposal, he may have a different
view.  The applicant had pushed the
development in the wrong direction and had condemned residents to
live in poorer conditions.  It was
necessary to look after residents who were going to live in these
flats.  He did not feel he was able to
support the application.  He added that
the comments from the Highway Authority were not a major
barrier.  The issue with the living
conditions was acknowledged in the report.
 
The
Chair invited the officer to respond to the comments
raised.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer responded that the increase in rooms
falling below the guidance was not from 10% to 30%.  There were more than the original scheme, but it
was not a significant increase.
 
Councillor G Saffery commented that previously when the
application had been considered the committee had been looking at
the full scheme.  Members had not been
happy with it.  The officer had
recommended rejecting the application which the committee had
agreed to do.  The appeal decision had
been disappointing.  He had reviewed the
variation and did not consider it to be a significant
change.  If it were to be refused there
a risk that it could be overturned on appeal again and may be
considered to be an unreasonable decision.  This could risk costs against the
council.  He said that he was not
prepared to gamble with public money. 
The variation seemed to be relatively minor.  Councillor Bashir agreed with these
comments.
 
Councillor Sharpe referred to the appeal decision.  He noted that 84 of the proposed flats had not met
the BRE guidance and there were multiple amenity
failures.  However, the Inspector had
placed a high weight on the communal facilities
available.  These facilities still
applied.  The fundamental principles of
the scheme had been established by the Planning
Inspector.  The concerns raised by
Councillor Martins had been covered in the Inspector’s
report.  The scheme had not
fundamentally changed.
 
Councillor A Saffery acknowledged that the committee’s
hands were tied.  However, she had
serious concerns about the developer and how they had not taken
care of the site.  She asked whether
there was anything that could be done to make sure they took
responsibility during the development.
 
The
officer advised that the Environmental Health team would respond to
any issues about anti-social behaviour. 
The applicant was required to submit a Construction Management
Plan, which should mitigate any harm to residents.
 
Councillor Basir agreed that the anti-social behaviour problems
have been a massive part of the problems with this
site.  He had listened to Mr Bennett and
agreed with his comments.  He questioned
whether there was anything in the council’s powers to enable
the site to be secured.
 
The
officer responded that he was not aware of any powers.  The planning element was constrained by the
Planning Inspector’s decision.
 
There
was a further comment about the current application and the issues
with the site.  The Chair stated that
this was a variation application and not a brand new
one.  The conditions had already been
determined by the Inspector.  The
officer confirmed that as this was a variation application and
therefore could only amend the two relevant conditions.  The council could not go beyond that.  It would not be considered reasonable.  He hoped that the applicant would hear the
comments made at this meeting and start the development.
 
All
members sympathised with the residents and the problems generated
by this site.  However, it was not
something this committee had any control over.  Any concerns needed to be raised with the Police
or Environmental Health and Community Protection within the
council.
 
There
was a further question about requiring hoarding round the
site.  The Chair noted that there was
fencing already but it was not being maintained.  He understood that it was not within the powers of
the committee to impose.  Councillor G
Saffery commented that it was important to remember who had
responsibility for maintaining the site.
 
Councillor Bashir asked whether it was possible for the
council’s officers to write to the developer stating that the
committee would welcome something to be put in place around the
site.  The Chair advised that this would
be within the responsibility of Environmental Health to contact the
developer.  Councillor Martins agreed
with the comments and that the developer needed to be told to
properly secure the site before they start building.  He asked whether it could be added as an
information item on the decision.  The
Chair noted that this was not a material consideration.  This was acknowledged by members, but it was felt
an information note would be useful.
 
The
officer responded that once building works were under way, he was
sure that the developer would install proper hoarding.  With regards to the original permission, the
commencement date had not yet expired. 
The developer wanted the decision on the variation to be made so
they could start the works on site.
 
The
Chair thanked everyone for their contributions.  He asked Councillor G Saffery to contact
Environmental Health about the state of the site and
fencing.  The neglected site was well
known by members.  The best the
committee could do within its powers was to consider the variation
application.  Members were constrained
by the Planning Inspector’s previous decision and the wording
provided by the county Highways Authority was not strong enough for
the proposal to be rejected.  He invited
the committee to vote on the officer’s recommendation as set
out in the report.
 
On
being put to the committee the application was approved.

Pre-commencement

 

3.         No
development, including demolition, shall commence until a
Demolition Environmental Management Plan (DEMP) has been submitted
to, and approved in writing by, the Local Planning Authority. The
DEMP must include details of:

a)    demolition
vehicle numbers, type, routing;

b)   access arrangements
to the site;

c)    traffic
management requirements;

d)   demolition and
storage compounds (including areas designated for car parking,
loading / unloading and turning areas);

e)    siting and
details of wheel washing facilities;

f)    cleaning of
site entrances, site tracks and the adjacent public
highway;

g)    timing of
demolition activities (including delivery times and removal of
waste) and to avoid school pick up/drop off times;

h)   provision of
sufficient on-site parking duplication;

i)
    where works cannot be
contained wholly within the site, a plan should be submitted
showing the site layout on the highway including extent of
hoarding, pedestrian routes and remaining road width for vehicle
movements;

j)     all air
quality mitigation measures consistent with the Air Quality
Assessment, dated 23 June 2022.
 

           
Thereafter the demolition of the development shall only be carried
out in accordance with the approved DEMP.

 

4.         No development
shall commence until an assessment of the risks posed by any
contamination has been submitted to, and approved in writing by,
the Local Planning Authority. This Risk Assessment must be
undertaken by a suitably qualified contaminated land practitioner,
in accordance with BS10175: Investigation of potentially
contaminated sites - Code of Practice and the Environment
Agency’s Model Procedures for the Management of Land
Contamination (CLR 11) (or equivalent British Standard and Model
Procedures if replaced), and shall assess any contamination on the
site, whether or not it originates on the site. The Assessment
shall include:

a)    a survey of
the extent, scale and nature of contamination;

b)   the potential risks
to:

·    
human health;

·    
property (existing or proposed) including buildings,
crops,

·    
livestock, pets, woodland and service lines and
pipes;

·    
adjoining land;

·    
ground waters and surface waters;

·    
ecological systems; and,

·    
archaeological sites and ancient
monuments
 

5.         (A) No
development shall take place where (following the Risk Assessment)
land affected by contamination is found which poses risks
identified as unacceptable in the Risk Assessment, until a detailed
Remediation Scheme has been submitted to, and approved in writing
by, the Local Planning Authority. The Scheme shall include an
appraisal of remediation options, identification of the preferred
option(s), the proposed remediation objectives and remediation
criteria, and a description and programme of the works to be
undertaken including the verification plan. The Scheme shall be
sufficiently detailed and thorough to ensure that upon completion
the site will not qualify as contaminated land under Part IIA of
the Environmental Protection Act 1990 in relation to its intended
use.

           
(B) The approved Scheme shall be carried out and upon completion a
Verification Report by a suitably qualified contaminated land
practitioner shall be submitted to, and approved in writing by, the
Local Planning Authority before the development is
occupied.
 

6.         No development
shall take place, excluding any demolition, until a detailed
Surface Water Drainage Scheme (SWDS) for the site, including the
details below based on the approved drainage strategy and
sustainable drainage principles, has been submitted to, and
approved in writing by, the Local Planning Authority. The SWDS must
include:

a)    a fully
detailed drainage strategy showing all SUDS/drainage features,
manholes and pipes, demonstrating how the entire site will be
drained including the access roads, basement ramp, roof surfaces
and shared/communal areas;

b)   detailed network
calculations (informed by FEH2022 rainfall data) for all rainfall
events up to and including the 1 in 100 year + 40% climate change
storm, including half drain down times;

c)    further
consideration of the proposed discharge rate to determine if a
restriction to greenfield runoff rates (or as close as is
practicable) is feasible;

d)   further
consideration of the feasibility of SUDS features such as permeable
paving, tree pits, rain gardens and swales to promote open,
multifunctional SUDS in preference to below-ground
storage;

e)    a detailed
assessment of how runoff quality treatment will be provided on site
for drainage from roads and parking, through the use of SUDS
features;

f)    detailed
ground investigations to confirm the height of groundwater on site,
in consideration of the proposed basement parking and belowground
drainage features such as attenuation tanks;

g)    detailed
engineered drawings of the proposed SUDS features including cross
section drawings, their size, volume, depth and any inlet and
outlet features including any connecting pipe runs; and,

h)   identification of
the exceedance flow paths for surface water for events greater than
the 1 in 100 year +40% climate change storm.

           
The SWDS shall subsequently be implemented in accordance with the
approved details before the development is completed.

 

7.         Development
shall not commence until details and a Method Statement for interim
and temporary drainage measures during the demolition and
construction phases have been submitted to, and approved in writing
by, the Local Planning Authority. This information shall provide
full details of who will be responsible for maintaining such
temporary systems and demonstrate how the site will be drained to
ensure there is no increase in the off-site flows, nor any
pollution, debris and sediment to any receiving watercourse or
sewer system. Where temporary discharges to a sewer are proposed,
written confirmation from the sewer owner that these have been
accepted shall be provided. The site works and construction phase
shall thereafter be carried out in accordance with approved Method
Statement.

 

8.         No
development, excluding demolition, shall commence until a
Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) has been
submitted to, and approved in writing by, the Local Planning
Authority.

           
The CEMP must include details of:

a)    construction
vehicle numbers, type, routing;

b)   access arrangements
to the site;

c)    traffic
management requirements;

d)   construction and
storage compounds (including areas designated for car parking,
loading / unloading and turning areas);

e)    siting and
details of wheel washing facilities;

f)    cleaning of
site entrances, site tracks and the adjacent public
highway;

g)    timing of
construction activities (including delivery times and removal of
waste) and to avoid school pick up/drop off times;

h)   provision of
sufficient on-site parking prior to commencement of construction
activities;

i)
    post construction
restoration/reinstatement of the working areas and temporary access
to the public highway;

j)     where
works cannot be contained wholly within the site a plan should be
submitted showing the site layout on the highway including extent
of hoarding, pedestrian routes and remaining road width for vehicle
movements;

k)    all air
quality mitigation measures consistent with the Air Quality
Assessment, dated 23 June 2022.
 

           
Thereafter the construction of the development shall only be
carried out in accordance with the approved CEMP.

 

Pre-specific part of development

 

9.         No works above
slab level shall commence until a detailed scheme for the off-site
highway improvement works has been submitted to, and approved in
writing by, the Local Planning Authority. The scheme shall reflect
drawing Ref 21473-CWA-ZZ-00-DR-A-0201-P-00 but be updated to
provide continuous footway crossover at the proposed access on St
John's Road. Prior to first occupation of the development, the
highways works shall be completed in accordance with the approved
details.
 

10.       Prior to first occupation
of the development, a Car Parking Management Plan (CPMP) shall be
submitted to, and approved in writing by, the Local Planning
Authority. The CPMP must include details of:

a)    car parking
allocation and distribution;

b)   the operation,
management, and implementation scheme for the car club, including a
minimum of five car club spaces and cars to be provided prior to
first occupation of any residential unit, and to be retained for a
minimum period of five years;

c)    methods to
prevent on-site car parking outside of the designated spaces,
including inappropriate parking within the layby;

d)   a timetable for
agreement of a monitoring plan regarding the implementation of the
CPMP; and,

e)    the provision
of active EV charging spaces and chargers (at minimum 20%) and
confirmation that all other spaces provide passive
infrastructure.

f)    how the
largest vehicles anticipated to use car parking spaces 61 –
76 can comfortably enter and exit the area in forward
gear.
 

11.       No external facing
materials shall be installed on the development until samples of
all external facing materials have been submitted to, and approved
in writing by, the Local Planning Authority. This shall include
obscure glazing to the two windows for the gym nearest the north
east corner of the courtyard. The relevant works shall thereafter
be carried out in accordance with the approved details.

 

Pre-occupation

 

12.       Prior to first occupation
of the development, details of both hard and soft landscape works
shall have been submitted to, and approved in writing by, the Local
Planning Authority. These details must include:

a)    the roof
gardens including irrigation systems;

b)   hardstanding
areas;

c)    soft
landscaping including tree planting;

d)   boundary
treatments;

e)    the
children’s play area;

f)    external
lighting;

g)    an extended
terrace to Flat Nu G.1; and,

h)   a Landscape
Management and Maintenance Plan.

           
The hard landscaping works shall be carried out in accordance with
the approved details prior to first occupation of the development.
The soft landscaping works shall be carried out in accordance with
the approved details not later than the first available planting
and seeding season after completion of development. Any trees or
plants whether new or existing which within a period of five years
die, are removed or become seriously damaged or diseased shall be
replaced in the next planting season with others of similar size
and species.

 

13.       No dwelling shall be first
occupied until the bin storage has been provided for the use of
residents, in accordance with the approved drawings. These
facilities shall be retained at all times for the use of the
residential occupiers of the dwellings.

 

14.       No part of the office
floorspace shall be first occupied until the bin storage has been
provided for the use of staff and visitors, in accordance with the
approved drawings. These facilities shall be retained at all times
for the use of the office occupiers.

 

15.       No dwelling shall be first
occupied until full details of the cycle storage for the
residential occupiers has been submitted to, and approved in
writing by, the Local Planning Authority. Details must include a
security scheme for the parking of cycles and the type of cycle
stands must also be clarified. The storage approved under this
condition shall be installed and made available for use prior to

times for cycle storage only and shall not be used for any other
purpose.

storage for the office occupiers has been submitted to, and
approved in writing by, the Local Planning Authority. Details must
include a security scheme for the parking of cycles and the type of
cycle stands must also be clarified. The storage approved under
this condition shall be installed and made available for use prior
to the first occupation of any part of office floorspace and shall
be retained at all times for cycle storage only and shall not be
used for any other purpose.

shall be first occupied until details of the proposed energy saving

in writing by, the Local Planning Authority. The measures shall be
based on those set out in the Energy and Sustainability Statement,
dated March 2022. Thereafter the construction of the development
shall only be carried out in accordance with the approved
details.

 

18.       No dwelling shall be first
occupied until the recommendations of the Noise Assessment, dated 8

full.

 

19.       The residential
development hereby approved shall not be first occupied until
details have been submitted to, and approved in writing by, the
Local Planning Authority to confirm that the dwellings have been
completed to meet the water efficiency requirement of 110 litres of
water per person per day.

 

20.       The office premises shall
not be first occupied until a scheme to obscure the glazing of some

submitted to, and approved in writing by, the Local Planning
Authority. The offices shall not be first occupied until the
scheme, as approved, has been carried out in full, and it shall be
retained thereafter.

of the development, a detailed Verification Report, appended with
substantiating evidence demonstrating the approved construction
details and specifications have been implemented in accordance with
the Surface Water Drainage Scheme, has been submitted to, and
approved in writing by, the Local Planning Authority.

           
The Verification Report shall include photographs of excavations
and soil profiles/horizons, any installation of any surface water
structure and control mechanism, as well as the
following:

a)    provision of a
complete set of as built drawings for site drainage;

b)   a management and
maintenance plan for the SUDS features and drainage network;
and,

c)    arrangements

details of any appointed management company.
 

For observation

 

22.       The offices premises shall
be used only as for offices within Classes E (g)(i) and shall be used for no other
purpose.

 

           
To protect the office use in the Clarendon Road Primary Office
Location pursuant to Policy EM4.3 of the Watford Local Plan
2021-2038.

found during the course of construction of the development that was
not previously identified shall be reported immediately to the
Local Planning Authority. Development on the part of the site
affected shall be suspended and a Risk Assessment carried out and
submitted to, and approved in writing by, the Local Planning
Authority. Where unacceptable risks are found, remediation and
verification schemes shall be submitted to, and approved in writing
by, the Local Planning Authority. These approved schemes shall be
carried out before the development is resumed or
continued.

 

24.       The development shall be
undertaken in accordance with the Drainage Strategy and
SuDS Assessment, dated 18 March 2022,
and must include the following measures:

a)    a safe
vehicular and pedestrian access through creation of an evacuation
plan to ensure vehicular access is maintained for emergency
services; and,

b)   finished floor
levels should be 300mm above the flood level of the 100 year plus
climate change event.

The following
motion had been proposed by Councillor Glen Saffery and seconded by
Mayor Peter Taylor:
 
“Council Notes:

·    
The NHS provides vital support every day. The NHS
staff at Watford General Hospital work tirelessly for patients
across our area.

·    
Mount Vernon Hospital, currently located in
Northwood, is a vital specialist healthcare provider in cancer and
related services, serving patients across Hertfordshire and North
London.

·    
Patients at Mount Vernon Hospital often face long
waits for transfers to neighbouring hospitals.

·    
Mount Vernon Hospital has launched a public
consultation regarding proposals to relocate services to
Watford: https://mvccreview.nhs.uk/

·    
Watford General Hospital is a key hospital but
requires substantial investment to meet current and future patient
needs.

·    
Before the general election, Labour politicians and
the local MP promised to rebuild Watford General Hospital. The
Government announced in January 2025 that construction of the new
hospital would not start until 2032 at the
earliest.

·    
Watford Borough Council has supported the Watford
General rebuild of the hospital. Actions include making land
available for the new facilities, delivering Thomas Sawyer Way to
improve access to the site and building the new multi-storey car
park. These actions have been key to clinicians identifying Watford
as the best location for this centre.

·    
A National Audit Office report this year indicated
that the Watford General rebuild will not be completed until
2038-39.
 
Council Believes:

·    
Relocating Mount Vernon to Watford would provide a
central, accessible location for patients, with excellent transport
links. The proposed relocation of cancer services to Watford
presents an opportunity to integrate specialist services with
existing local healthcare infrastructure.

·    
The Mount Vernon relocation would create a
world-class centre for cancer care and research, enabling more
clinical trials and faster access to new treatments. A new
sky-bridge would give cancer patients direct access to acute
services at Watford General.

·    
The best approach would be a combined redevelopment
of Watford General Hospital alongside the relocation. This would
create a modern, state-of-the-art healthcare facility. This would
improve services for patients across the region and potentially
accelerating the delivery of the much-needed new
hospital.

·    
Residents, patients, and staff deserve the best
health care facilities possible that were promised to them. They
have waited far too long for this investment.

·    
The government should combine these projects and
bring forward the redevelopment of Watford General. Construction of
the new hospital should start as soon as possible, ahead of the
current timeline.
 
Council Resolves:

·    
To formally support the relocation of Mount Vernon
Hospital to Watford.

·    
To share with residents and local businesses via a
communications plan the Mount Vernon relocation consultation that
is currently live: https://mvccreview.nhs.uk/

·    
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to write to the
Secretary of State for Health to express Watford Council’s
support for the Mount Vernon relocation plans, delivering this
alongside a redeveloped Watford General Hospital.

·    
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to formally support
the relocation plan by responding to the open
consultation.”

Members debated the motion.
 
On being put to Council the motion was
agreed.

The
following motion had been proposed by Councillor Ian Stotesbury and
seconded by Councillor Mark Hofman:
 
“This Council notes:

1.     
The "Rezone Watford Stations" campaign, launched by the Watford
Liberal Democrats, which has highlighted the significant financial
disparity faced by Watford commuters due to current rail
zoning.

2.     
That Watford’s stations are currently split across multiple,
inconsistent fare zones:

·      
Watford Metropolitan Line Station: Zone 7

·      
Watford High Street: Zone 8

·      
Bushey Station: Zone 8

·      
Watford Junction: Special Fares Zone

3.      A
peak return journey from Watford Junction currently costs
approximately £22.20—nearly double the cost of a peak
return from Zone 6 stations like Epping (£11.60), despite
being a similar distance (approx. 16.5 miles) from Central
London.

4.     
That this "outdated zoning classification" by TfL can cost a
Watford commuter over £1,000 extra per year compared to those
living in Zone 6.

5.     
The ongoing cost-of-living crisis is exacerbated for local residents by TfL fare increases (including the
5.8% increase in 2026), coupled with the return of office-working
mandates from some employers, making affordable transport a
critical economic issue for the town.

6.      In
a recent Freedom of Information response, TfL confirmed that it has
no current zoning policy. It also stated that decisions on the
zoning of individual Watford stations were made in the 1980s and
have since been ‘lost’.
           
This
Council believes:

1.     
The current zoning system is an absurd anomaly and is fundamentally
unfair to Watford residents who travel into London to work, study,
and support the economy.

2.     
Rezoning all Watford stations (including Bushey) into Zone 6 would
create a fairer, simpler fares system and put significant money
back into the pockets of local
residents.

3.     
Lowering the cost of rail travel would encourage greater use of
public transport, supporting the
council’s environmental goals and reducing carbon
emissions.

4.     
Watford's status as a major regional hub and its proximity to
London justifies its inclusion in the Zone 6 boundary, similar to other areas outside the M25 like Epping
or Elstree & Borehamwood.

5.     
Rezoning Watford will also have significant benefits to London
residents who regularly commute or travel to Watford.

6.      In
the interests of transparency, and as a taxpayer-funded body
responsible for transport, TfL has a public duty to maintain
up-to-date policies and make them available for public scrutiny
upon request.
           
This
Council resolves to:

1.     
Formally endorse the campaign to rezone all Watford stations
(Watford Junction, Watford High Street, Bushey, and Watford
Metropolitan) into TfL Zone 6.

2.     
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to write to the Secretary of State
for Transport, the Commissioner of TfL, and the Mayor of London (as
Chair of TfL) urging them to:

·      
Initiate an urgent independent review of the zoning
for Watford’s stations.

·      
Work collaboratively to end the “special
fare” status of Watford Junction in favour of a Zone 6
classification.

·      
Provide a clear timeline for the reclassification to
ensure Watford residents receive a “fair deal” on
travel.

3.     
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to share a copy of this motion
with the local Members of Parliament for Watford and South West Hertfordshire, seeking their active
support in Westminster for this change.”

amendment to the motion was proposed by Councillor Asif Khan and
seconded by Councillor Bell.  Prior to

8.     
That any review of rail zoning should consider the wider transport
corridor and stations located between Watford and the current Zone
6 boundary, including stations such as Carpenders Park,
Rickmansworth and Moor Park, to ensure that any potential rezoning
is considered fairly and strategically across the
network.

 
This
Council believes:

1.         
The current zoning system is an absurd anomaly and
is fundamentally unfair to Watford residents who travel into London
to work, study, and support the economy.

2.         
Rezoning all Watford stations (including Bushey)
into Zone 6 would create a fairer, simpler fares system and put
significant money back into the pockets of local residents.

3.         
Lowering the cost of rail travel would encourage
greater use of public transport, supporting the council’s environmental goals
and reducing carbon emissions.

4.         
Watford's status as a major regional hub and its
proximity to London justifies its inclusion in the Zone 6 boundary,
similar to other areas outside the M25
like Epping or Elstree & Borehamwood.

5.         
Rezoning Watford will also have significant benefits
to London residents who regularly commute or travel to
Watford.

6.         
In the interests of transparency, and as a
taxpayer-funded body responsible for transport, TfL has a public
duty to maintain up-to-date policies and make them available for
public scrutiny upon request.

7.     
That meaningful progress on rail fare reform will require
collaboration between Transport for London, Hertfordshire County
Council as the strategic transport authority, neighbouring local
authorities and local Members of Parliament.
 

This Council resolves to:

1.         
Formally endorse the campaign to rezone all Watford
stations (Watford Junction, Watford High Street, Bushey, and
Watford Metropolitan) into TfL Zone 6.

2.         
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to write to the
Secretary of State for Transport, the Commissioner of TfL, and the
Mayor of London (as Chair of TfL) urging them to:

· 
   Initiate an
urgent independent review of the zoning for Watford’s
stations.

· 
   Work
collaboratively to end the “special fare” status of
Watford Junction in favour of a Zone 6 classification.

· 
   Provide a clear
timeline for the reclassification to ensure Watford residents
receive a “fair deal” on travel.

3.     
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to also write to Hertfordshire
County Council as the strategic transport authority, and
neighbouring councils including Three Rivers District Council and
Hertsmere Borough Council, inviting them to work collaboratively on
a wider review of rail fare zoning affecting Watford and
surrounding stations.

4.     
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to share a copy of this motion
with the local Members of Parliament for Watford, South West Hertfordshire and neighbouring
constituencies, seeking their active support in Parliament for a
fair and transparent review of rail fare zoning affecting Watford
and the surrounding area.
topline: The Council has decided to endorse a campaign to rezone all Watford stations into TfL Zone 6 to address financial disparities faced by commuters.

The
following motion had been proposed by Councillor Asif Khan and
seconded by Councillor Nigel Bell:
 
“This Council notes that:
 

·      
Since 28 February 2026, a major international
conflict has escalated following joint military strikes by the
United States and Israel on Iran, which has led to a widening
regional war and retaliatory attacks across the Middle
East.

·      
The conflict has caused loss of life, regional
instability and growing international concern about further
escalation.

·      
Events of this scale can have a profound emotional
impact on communities here in the United Kingdom, including
residents in Watford who may have family, cultural or faith
connections to the region.

·      
Global conflicts can sometimes create tension or
misunderstanding locally if not addressed through calm leadership
and strong community relationships.

·      
Watford is a town built on diversity, mutual respect
and strong inter-faith cooperation, where people of many
backgrounds and beliefs live side by side.
 
This
Council believes that:
 

·      
Watford’s diversity is one of the town’s
greatest strengths and must always be protected and
celebrated.

·      
International conflicts must never be allowed to
divide communities in Watford or Hertfordshire.

·      
At times of global tension, civic leaders, faith
leaders and community organisations have an important
responsibility to promote unity, understanding and calm.

·      
The strength of Watford lies in its long tradition
of neighbourliness, respect and cooperation between different
communities.
 
This
Council resolves to:
 

·      
Reaffirm that Watford is a welcoming, inclusive and
united town for people of all faiths, backgrounds and
cultures.

·      
Work with local faith leaders, community groups,
Hertfordshire Constabulary and voluntary organisations to promote
dialogue, understanding and community cohesion.

·      
Encourage and support interfaith initiatives and
community events that bring residents together during periods of
global tension.

·      
Send a clear message that hatred, racism,
antisemitism, Islamophobia and all forms of prejudice have no place
in Watford.

·      
Stand alongside community leaders across Watford and
Hertfordshire in promoting peace, respect and unity.
 
This
Council further affirms that, whatever events unfold
internationally, the people and leaders of Watford will remain
united in protecting the harmony, safety and cohesion of our
town.”

purpose:
Erection of a first floor rear and side
extension with the side extension not extending beyond the existing
