content:
The
committee received a report of the Planning Officer, which set out
details of the application.  It was
noted that there had been nine objections to the
proposal.
 
The
Development Management Lead introduced the report, providing
details of the location site, the existing building and the
proposed application.  She explained
that the application was being presented to the committee due to
the number of objections that had been received.  She advised that the application did not include a
change of use of the property; the application was solely for
extensions to the existing building.   
 
The
Chair asked the officer to explain the rules about Houses in
Multi-Occupation (HMO). 
 
The
Development Management Lead explained that permitted development
rights were set by national government and not the local
authority.  Any unrestricted property
could have up to six separate individuals living in a property
without the need to seek planning permission.  In response to a follow up question from the
Chair, the Development Management Lead confirmed that the national
rules specified that once a seventh person was expected to occupy
the property planning permission would be required.  There were also rules about licensing HMOs which
was separate to planning. 
 
Councillor Sharpe sought assurance from the officer that the
committee had to consider the application at face value, as applied
for, and that no weight should be given to what it could become in
the future.  The officer confirmed that
this was correct.
 
The
Chair added that the rules regarding the level of occupancy for
HMOs had been increased by the government before planning
permission was required. He invited Saskia Hardijzer to speak to the committee against the
application.
 
Ms
Hardijzer thanked the committee for
allowing her to speak about the application.  She asked members to reject the application based
on planning grounds, the Local Plan policies and the principles of
the National Planning Policy Framework. 
She referred to the policies and explained why she felt the
application failed to meet the requirements.  Firstly, she stressed it was not about personal
matters or speculation about the future but the
development.  She spoke about the size
of the property and its proportions; she considered the application
failed the test.  The proposal was to
extend it to a six-bedroom, five-bathroom property and therefore
the overall view would not make the extensions subordinate and
would give an overall terracing effect. 
It was not in keeping with the overall character of the
area.  The extension breached the
45-degree line, causing loss of light and overshadowing to the
neighbouring property.  The upper floor
windows would overlook the neighbouring property.  The property would increase from a four-bedroom
property to six-bedrooms, a substantial increase to the
property.   She said the committee
needed to consider the real world
impacts.  There would be a higher level
of occupancy on this site than a typical family dwelling in this
area.  The intensification was a
material planning consideration.
 
Ms
Hardijzer then referred to parking and
the highway.  She said that Coningesby Drive was a narrow residential road and
a route to recreational facilities. 
There was limited off street parking at the property.  Even though technical specifications would be met,
members should consider the realities, including modest increase in
parking, congestion and pedestrian safety.
 
Ms
Hardijzer spoke about policy H8 and the
protection of the character of the area.  She described the local area and the low level of
occupation intensity.  The proposal was
materially different to the area.  This
could harm the character.  She said that
members should consider what was being built and the impact it
would create.
 
Ms
Hardijzer explained that as a direct
neighbour of the applicant she had been in contact with
them.  The applicant had advised that
the property had been purchased as a family home, but his family
had been absent which had added to concerns the property would be
used for business use.  It was not
suitable for commercial use and would be out of keeping for the
structure of the house and neighbourhood.  This was the third application that had been
submitted and it was understood that fewer objections had been made
on this occasion.  However,
objectors’ major concerns related to building control
compliance.  Previous complaints by
neighbours had not been properly addressed.  There were also concerns about the use of
contractors who had raised residents’ concerns about
questionable practices by them.  She
finished by asking members that, if planning permission were
granted, there would be a strict oversight to ensure that works
were carried out within planning compliance and building
regulations.   There should be
proper consideration for neighbours. 
The proposal represented an overdevelopment of a modest
semi-detached plot, causing unacceptable harm to neighbours’
amenities and parking concerns.  For
these reasons it was contrary to the Local Plan.
           
The
Chair thanked Ms Hardijzer for her
comments.  He asked the Development
Management Lead to respond to the comments about intensification of
the site, highways concerns and the proposal being out of
character.  He also asked her to explain
what controls could be put in place.
 
The
Development Management Lead said that regarding intensification, it
was currently one dwelling and was proposed to remain one
dwelling.  In the Cassiobury area it was
common for properties to be extended and extra bedrooms
added.  If it was a new dwelling or
there was a change to multiple dwellings that would be considered
an intensification.  In terms of parking
requirements, those specified were maximums and had not been
required due to the addition of more rooms.   The overall character could be a subjective
issue.  It was necessary to consider the
plot size and footprint of houses in the area.  She referred to the Residential Design Guide which
provided information on how extensions should be scaled and
designed.  For example, side extensions
should be less than half the width of the house.  There were other matters to be
considered.  Based on the guidance,
officers had assessed the proposal was largely compliant and fully
compliant on the side extension.  It was
not out of context with other properties in the street.  She then explained that Building Regulations were
separate to planning requirements.  The
contractor would be a matter for the Building Inspector to
consider.   In the application
there was advice to the applicant about Environmental Health
regulations and working hours.  In
planning terms, officers were looking at the visual and amenity
impacts.
 
The
Chair invited Mr Rehan Shahid to speak to the committee.
 
Mr
Shahid informed members that he was the applicant.  He wished to address the objections, which he felt
were about the design and use.  The
design had been addressed in the planning officer’s
report.  The proposal met the
Residential Design Guide.  It was a
proportionate size and was sympathetic to the design of the
surrounding area.  It would not affect
the sunlight or daylight of the neighbouring occupiers.  He repeated that this had been covered in the
officer’s report.  Based on this
he felt the design concerns had been addressed.
 
Mr
Shahid advised that he wished to speak about the use of the
property and concerns raised.  He said
that this was also covered in the officer’s report and that
no change of use had been proposed.  He
explained that he jointly owned the property with his
wife.  He had a normal residential
mortgage.  The property would be the
family home for the long term.  It had
been chosen due to its location, schools and access to
transport.  All these factors had been
taken into account before the house had
been purchased.  The intention was to
make this a family home that was suitable for them for a long
time.  All rules and guideline had been
considered to make sure there was minimal impact on the neighbours,
which was clarified in the design statement.  They had tried to make sure that they had
facilitated all they could and still make it a home that worked for
the family.  He asked the committee to
make a decision based on the presented
facts. 
 
The
Chair thanked Mr Shahid and opened the meeting up to members’
questions and comments.
 
Councillor Bell began by thanking both speakers and the
Development Management Lead.  Overall,
he had no objection to the proposal but did feel it was wrong to
say that the Residential Design Guide had not been
exceeded.   It was clear it had
been exceeded but was considered in proportion.  Looking at other properties in the area, the
proposed development would not be out of character.  He was unable to identify any reasons to object to
the application.
 
Councillor Johnson agreed with Councillor Bell’s
comments.  He was unable to see any
reasons to reject it.  It was
substantially different, but he hoped the applicant would do all he
could to accommodate his neighbours and be sympathetic to any
concerns they had.  He could not see any
reason to refuse it.  He added that if
the committee did refuse the application, he felt that the Planning
Inspector would approve it anyway.
 
The
Chair reminded everyone that the Residential Design Guide was a
guidance for applicants.  It was not an
absolute.
 
Councillor G Saffery noted that there had been reference to
previous applications.  He asked the
officer for more details.
 
The
Development Management Lead confirmed that previous applications
had been submitted, but they had been withdrawn before they were
determined.  The previous proposal had
been larger.  This revised application
had been submitted with a smaller extension.
 
Councillor Sharpe commented that over the last 10 years the
government had changed planning rules, enabling an increase in the
size of houses without planning permission being
required.  He was referring to permitted
development rights.
 
The
Development Management Lead explained the government rules
regarding semi-detached houses, which were allowed a single storey
extension up to six metres at the rear, as long
as there were no adverse impacts on neighbours.  She outlined the other rules including for side
boundaries and loft conversions.
 
The
Chair thanked everyone for their contributions and based on the
committee’s comments, it would appear
that they would be supporting the officer’s
recommendation.  He said that the
neighbouring resident’s concerns had been
understood.  He advised that if they did
encounter any issues, they would be able to raise their
concerns.
 
The
Chair invited the committee to vote on the officer’s
recommendation set out in the report.
 
On
being put to the committee the application was approved.
 
Resolved –
 
That,
planning permission be granted subject to the conditions listed
below:
 

Conditions
 

1.         The
development to which this permission relates shall be begun within
a period of three years commencing on the date of this
permission.

 

2.         The
development shall be carried out in accordance with the following
drawings, unless otherwise approved in writing by the Local

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Planning Policy Officer which provided the
Biodiversity Report for 2026 as required by
legislation.  Members were asked to note
the content of the report.
 
The Mayor invited Councillor Stotesbury to
introduce the report.
 
Councillor Stotesbury informed members that the report was about the work
being undertaken to “consider, conserve and enhance”
biodiversity.  It was not about new
actions, as those would be in other policies.  The report was a summary of the things the council
had been doing across all policies related to
biodiversity.  It included information
about the partnership working that had taken place.  The reporting period had been selected as the
government had been looking biodiversity net gain in relation to
planning.  It was timely as the current
government was considering changes and potential exemptions for
developers.  Lastly, he wished to thank
the officers for their work including the Planning Policy Officer
who was present at the meeting.
 
The
Mayor added his thanks to the officers.
 
Councillor Williams said he endorsed all Councillor
Stotesbury’s comments.  It was a
good report and he welcomed the point
that stakeholders had been included.
 
The
Mayor said he echoed Councillor Stotesbury’s comments all the
different groups that had been involved, including Friends groups,
volunteers.  The council was fortunate
to have so many people involved.  The
Mayor invited Cabinet to vote on the recommendation in the
report.
 
Resolved –
 
that
the contents of the report and the Biodiversity Duty Report 2026
are noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Biodiversity Duty Report for 2026.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Delivery Support Lead, Intelligence,
Performance and Improvement Lead and Community Commissioning Lead,
which provided the latest quarter’s update on the Council
Plan, Delivery Plan, external key performance indicators, voluntary
sector commissioning framework metrics and key corporate
strategies. As this was the last report during the life of the
current Delivery Plan, a summary of activity over the last two
years was also included.
 
The Mayor thanked the officers for their work in
producing this report.  He outlined some
of the achievements over the last quarter.  These included the car club which continued to
grow; the number of EV charging points continuing to increase; the
£3 million investment in Central leisure centre improvements
and the works at Woodside.  At the last
Cabinet members had agreed to the appointment of the Innovation and
Incubation Hub operator.  He then
referred to the key performance indicators.  He was pleased to see that progress was being made
on littering and the response times on fly tipping.  He added that both he and Councillor Pattinson
often commented on the housing figures; the temporary housing
figures had levelled and the number of people sleeping rough had
fallen, which was probably in part due to the winter night shelter,
which was funded by the council and done in partnership with New
Hope.  The report contained a lot of
positive information.  He noted it would
be forwarded to Overview and Scrutiny Committee.
           
The Mayor invited Cabinet to vote on the
recommendations.
 
Resolved –
 

1.         that Cabinet notes
the progress updates within this report over the last two years of
the Delivery Plan 2024/26, including in relation to:

·       
the Council Plan 2022-26 and Delivery Plan 2024 -26
(Appendix A)

·       
the external key performance indicator results for
Quarter 3 of 2025/26 (Appendix B)

·       
the Voluntary Sector Commissioning Framework metrics
for Quarter 3 of 2025/26 (Appendix C)

·       
the council’s key corporate strategies
(Appendix D)
 

2.         that
Cabinet notes that the progress updates relating to the Delivery
Plan, key performance indicators and key corporate strategies will
be presented to Overview and Scrutiny Committee in March
2026.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve progress updates on the Council Plan, Delivery Plan, and key performance indicators.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Delivery Support Lead which provided the
latest update on the council’s Corporate Risk
Register.
 
The
Mayor invited Councillor Begum to introduce the report.
 
Councillor Begum explained that Corporate Risk Register adopted
previously set out how the council managed risk.  In line with the strategy, it was presented to
Cabinet quarterly.   It was
important to robustly manage risks. 
Ongoing overview of the risks ensured the council was proactively
managing issues, identifying mitigation measures or addressing the
risks.  The document is regularly
reviewed by officers and members and there been no changes to
existing risk scores since the last report.  However, there were some new risks and these had been explained in the report,
covering social engineering, the introduction the use of AI within
the council and the pressures from Local Government Reorganisation
(LGR).  She added that the council had
invested in training on AI, cybersecurity and data protection for
all staff.  She also mentioned the
pressure on the housing service and that actions had been
undertaken to overcome the risk.  
Oversight of the document remained with Audit Committee and would
be presented at their next meeting.
 
The
Mayor thanked Councillor Begum for the update.  He was not surprised that AI and LGR had been
added to the register.  He invited
Cabinet to vote on the recommendations set out in the
report.
 
           
Resolved –
 

1.         that the
Corporate Risk Register has been reviewed and noted.

 

2.         that the
proposed amendments to the Corporate Risk Register have been
reviewed and noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to review and approve recommendations on the council's Corporate Risk Register.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Associate Director of Customer and
Corporate Services, which set out the latest update of the AI
policy following its recent review.
 
The
Mayor invited Councillor Hill to introduce the report.
 
Councillor Hill explained that the policy was reviewed every six
months, having previously been agreed by Cabinet in September
2024.  This was good practice due to the
rapid changes in this area.  There were
a few key changes which she explained. 
These included the use of permitted tools and additional safeguards
for customer facing AI interactions. 
The policy supported innovation and ensured users understood their
responsibilities and the difference between secure corporate tools
and open-source AI platforms.  AI was
increasingly being used in the council and across local
government.  She asked members to
support the recommendations.
 
The
Mayor noted earlier discussions about the use of AI and how it was
benefitting residents.
 
Councillor Stotesbury said there were lots of reasons to use
AI.  However, privacy was important for
residents.
 
The
Mayor invited members to vote on the recommendation within the
report.
 
Resolved –
 
That
the updated AI Policy has been reviewed and is approved.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the updated AI policy following its recent review.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Customer Service Delivery Manager which
provided an update to existing guidance and policy.
 
The Mayor invited Councillor Hill to introduce
the report.
 
Councillor Hill explained that the documents had
been renamed to better reflect their content and help staff in
using them.  They had been reviewed to
ensure they were clear and consistent, including best safeguarding
practices, ensuring the safety of staff, members and the
public.  There was also a better
understanding of escalation practices. Officers had spoken to
similar customer-facing organisations, including Watford Community
Housing and Citizens Advice Watford, to ensure the policies
reflected best practice.
 
The Mayor acknowledged previous discussions on
this important piece of work. 
Thankfully cases were rare, but it was important there was a clear
policy.  He invited Cabinet to vote on
the recommendations.
 
Resolved –
           

1.         that the
updated Potentially Violent Persons Guidance and Unreasonable
Behaviour and Contact Restrictions Policy is approved.

 

2.         that it
is noted the policies have been benchmarked against other local
authority approaches and renamed to improve clarity, consistency
and tone.

 

3.         that it
is noted that the policies may require further review and update
should the council proceed with the introduction of an
organisation-wide lone worker safety solution, such as SoloProtect.
topline: The Mayor has decided to approve updated guidance and policy on potentially violent persons and unreasonable behaviour.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Monitoring Officer which sought member
approval for the council’s vote regarding the new Business
Improvement District (BID) ballot that was currently
underway. 
 
The
Mayor advised that the report had been discussed at the last
Council meeting.  He repeated that he
was a non-voting observer on the BID Board and had confirmed with
the Monitoring Officer that he could vote on this item.  He paid tribute to the BID team for all the work
they were doing.  There had been a lot
of positives achieved in the Town Centre.  There had been a high response rate in the last
ballot.  The vision for the new BID was
set out in the report.  The team had
worked closely with businesses along Clarendon Road to ensure it
was understood what they wanted for the future.  He explained that the council also had a vote as a
business rates payer on Clarendon Road.
 
Councillor Dychton said that it was important to work with the
businesses along Clarendon Road.  It was
also a great opportunity for local community groups who wanted to
engage with businesses along that road. 
She looked forward to seeing the positive outcomes of this new
agreement.
 
The
Mayor invited members to vote on the recommendation.
 
Resolved –
 
That
the Chief Operating Officer is authorised to vote ‘Yes’
in relation to the council’s vote as a National Non Domestic
Rates (NNDR) levy payer in the Watford Clarendon BID
ballot.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the recommendation to vote 'Yes' in the Watford Clarendon BID ballot.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Chief Executive which provided a
reflective review of the council’s performance and
achievements over the past four years.
 
The
Mayor thanked officers for this update, which was an excellent
piece of work summarising the breadth of work the council had
done.  He highlighted some of the
achievements.   He noted that the
council had already implemented or was on track to deliver 95% of
the commitments.  Often people were
sceptical of manifesto pledges, but this showed what had been
achieved and was regularly monitored. 
He commented that it was not just the council stating it had
achieved the commitments, but it was recognised through the awards
that been achieved, including iESE Council of the Year.  There had been lots of recognition for the
council’s work.  The document also
included residents’ views and what they wanted for the
future.  There were case studies, which
again showed the breadth of work.  He
had also received direct positive feedback about the work of one
particular member of staff.
 
The
Chief Executive said that it was important to carry out this review
at the end of the four years.  It
reflected how much a local authority could achieve, even though
over the four years there had been significant financial pressures,
rising demands from the public and pressures from LGR.  She stated that it was not just the council saying
these things, but that it had been recognised
nationally.  She added her thanks to all
the staff that made this happen.  She
hoped that they would take this forward into LGR, shaping the
future the council for Watford residents in the future.
 
The
Mayor echoed the Chief Executive’s comments, particularly
about the staff.
 
Councillor Dychton said that she was proud of Watford and what
had been achieved over the last four years, particularly community
engagement.  The relationship with
officers over the last four years had been amazing.   When she had attended community meetings or
met community groups, everyone said the same and that Watford was
such a welcoming place and there was the ability to collaborate
with each other.  She thanked officers,
especially from the community portfolio who were constantly working
to make sure the council delivered for its resident and their
voices were heard.
 
The
Mayor invited Cabinet to vote on the recommendation.
 
Resolved –
 
That
the Council Review 2022–2026 is noted and its publication is
endorsed as a summary of progress, performance and achievements
under the current Council Plan.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to endorse the Council Review 2022-2026, highlighting progress and achievements under the current Council Plan.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Parks and Greenspaces Development Lead
which provided a 10-year plan for the Green Spaces
Strategy.  Members were asked to approve
the Strategy.
 
The Mayor invited Councillor Williams to
introduce the report.
 
Councillor Williams began by informing Cabinet
that the new strategy was an ambitious 10-yer plan that was
building on everything that had already been achieved and the
investment in green spaces.  Residents
enjoyed the open spaces which included allotments, parks and
woodlands.  In addition to making
Watford greener, it also made it fairer, healthier and more
connected.  He thanked officers for
their hard work.  There had been wide
consultation with various stakeholders and local groups and views
had been incorporated into the strategy.  Once the 217-page technical strategy had been
approved, it would be consolidated into a 20-page non-technical
document.  Watford residents loved the
green spaces locally.  There were strong
foundations due to the previous investment and this strategy would
propel the town forward for future generations. 
 
Councillor Stotesbury thanked Councillor Williams
and the officers.  The investment in
green spaces showed the council did not rest and was a legacy for
the future.  He had identified parks
that he had not yet visited.  The
strategy covered all green spaces and proposed making other areas
greener.  Health and understanding
residents’ needs had also been considered in the development
of the strategy.  It showed how
investing in green spaces and the natural world could help
people’s wellbeing.  He was
pleased to see the document and the ambition moving
forward. 
 
Councillor Pattinson said she wanted to refer to
the wellbeing aspects and welcomed the focus on inclusivity in the
strategy.  Disability Watford had been
involved in the design.  She noted that
in the Delivery Plan it would be useful to link some of the
wellbeing aspects to the deliverables, monitoring the positive
impact.
 
The Parks and Greenspaces Development Lead
advised that health data was taken into account.  The team worked closely with the Sports and
Physical Activity Development Manager on the sports and wellbeing
programmes.  The sports and health
documents had also been updated and ran alongside this
strategy.  Officers would monitor and
provide feedback on the Delivery Plan.
 
Councillor Williams highlighted the new
additional Park Run in Holywell.  These
events encouraged people to come out and join in.  He noted that some people walked instead of
running.  He wanted the council’s
parks to be as accessible as possible for all
individuals.  He provided the example of
the perimeter paths that had been installed at Lea Farm
Park.  The strategy promoted healthy
living and accessibility for all.
 
The Mayor agreed that the improvements at Lea
Farm had been welcomed by residents.
 
Councillor Dychton noted the reference to the new
Park Run.  She had heard from residents
and it had been well received.  Over 200
people had taken part and they were looking forward to seeing how
it would expand in the future.
 
The Mayor advised that he had attended the first
run.  He asked officers about the
changes that the residents would notice as a result of the
strategy.
 
The Parks and Greenspaces Development Lead
replied that they would see the aims to increase the accessible
play equipment.  The 20-page document
would set out the strategy’s aims and objectives and would
not be as academic as they were in the main strategy.  Engagement had continued with the stakeholders in
the parks.  The check-ins for the Park
Runs had provided an insight into the audience.  There was also the work with
councillors.  In addition, as projects
were developed further engagement would take
place.
 
The Director of Sustainability, Environment and
Communities added that as Councillor Stotesbury had mentioned, the
brief summary document may highlight parks to residents that they
were not aware of previously.   It
would hopefully encourage residents to access the parks and enjoy
the health and wellbeing benefits.
 
Councillor Stotesbury added that the work that
had gone into the documents would also underpin planning decisions
and policies.  The strategy provides the
council to identify where facilities were lacking and as grant
funding came forward focus it on those areas.  The evidence base was clear.
 
The Mayor added his thanks to the officers for
their work.  The strategy had
highlighted the spread of parks across the town and also places
where there could be improvement in the future.  He invited members to vote on the recommendation
in the report.
 
Resolved –
 
that
the Greenspaces Strategy 2025-2035 is approved.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the 10-year Green Spaces Strategy for Watford, aiming to make the town greener, fairer, healthier, and more connected.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Planning Policy Officer including the
Authority Monitoring Report for 2024/25.  The Monitoring Report outlined the progress made
against targets and indicators that assessed the effectiveness of
the Watford Local Plan 2021-2038 policies.
 
The Mayor invited Councillor Saffery to introduce
the report.
 
Councillor Saffery informed members that the
report was a way to assess the Local Plan policies and not about
the state of the council.  It was a way
to check if there were other measures needed to support the
policies and their delivery.   He
advised that the council was at the mercy of broader social and
economic trends.  For example, the
council could not compel developers to build.  He highlighted some of the headline data in the
report.  He said that there was more
affordable and social housing coming through and the commuted sums
to support this.  Finally, he thanked
the officers, particularly the Planning Policy Officer, for the
work in bringing this report together and their support in
delivering the Local Plan.
 
The Mayor commented the report was always useful
to see and the data and information it contained.
 
Councillor Stotesbury said that the report showed
that the Local Plan that had been approved was delivering as
required.  He referred to the tough
decision about where buildings should be put in
order to meet the high housing target.  The decision had been to build on brownfield sites
near train stations.  The council
listened to what the government wanted and then it got on to
deliver.  The data in the document
reflected this.
 
Councillor Stotesbury and the Mayor
agreed.
 
Councillor Pattinson referred to the
accessibility of developments.  She
considered 10% of major development was something the council
should be proud of, as it helped to meet the needs of a growing
resident population.
 
The Mayor said that recently he had met a group
of residents on this subject.  It was
positive to see in order to meet the
growing demand.  He invited Cabinet to
vote on the recommendation.
 
Resolved –
 
that
Cabinet agrees to publish the Authority Monitoring Report 2024/25,
as included in Appendix 1 of the report, on the council’s
website.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the publication of the Authority Monitoring Report 2024/25 for the Watford Local Plan policies

purpose:
Erection of two 50-seater stands within the
boundary of the fenced-in outdoor football pitch.
content:
The
committee received a report of the Principal Planning Officer
setting out the application requesting approval for two 50-seater
stands within the boundary of the fenced-in outdoor football
pitch.
 
The
Principal Planning Officer introduced the report.  She explained that the application was being
presented to the committee due to the number of complaints that had
been received.  She highlighted the site
of the football pitch in comparison to the residential
properties.  The stands would be located
on the side nearest the neighbouring school, enclosed within the
pitch.  The site was mostly screened
from the A41 by trees.  The capacity of
this pitch would not be increased from the previously agreed
capacity.  The site had a car
park and a Travel Plan had been agreed
previously.  The Highways Authority had
no objection to the proposal.  In
summary the proposal would enhance the facilities on site and would
have no impact on the closest residential properties. 
 
There
were no question from the committee for
the officer.  The Chair invited
Councillor Asif Khan to speak to the committee.
 
Councillor Khan thanked the committee and advised that he was a
ward councillor for this area.  The
football club was named after a previous councillor and sports
centre that had been located here.  This
was a well
established club. 
However, he was aware of the concerns raised by
residents.  He considered the proposal
to be a modest well considered enhancement.  There would be no additional impact on residents,
as the stands were inside the current pitch.  The stands were required to meet Football
Association ground rules.  This was due
to the promotion of the team.  In
planning terms, the stands were lower than the existing
fencing.  There would be no
intensification of use.  The club also
gave back to the community by allowing visitors to the Mosque to
use the car park.  This was a local club
requesting an improvement to its facilities.  He asked the committee to support the
officer’s recommendation.
 
The
Chair thanked Councillor Khan for his comprehensive
comments.  The Chair noted some
residents had concerns.  He invited the
committee to make comments or ask the officer questions.
 
Members
welcomed the application and acknowledged the success of the
football club which should be celebrated.  They noted that there had been no concerns raised
by Highways.  The stand provided seating
for those that required it.
 
The
Chair invited the committee to vote on the officer’s
recommendation set out in the report.
 
On
being put to the committee the application was approved.
 
Resolved –
 
That,
planning permission be granted subject to the conditions listed
below:
 

Conditions
 
1.
       
Time limit
 

           
The development to which this permission relates shall be begun
within a period of three years commencing on the date of this
permission.

 

2.         Approved
drawings and documents

 

           
The development hereby permitted shall be carried out in accordance
with the following approved drawings and documents:
 

           
821-331 / DWG /0010 01

           
821-331 / DWG /0003 01

           
ELEVATION AND PLAN PROPOSED (FRONT, REAR, SECTION, 3D VIEW, PLAN
VIEW)

 

3.         Construction
Management Plan

 

           
No development shall commence until a Construction Management Plan
has been submitted to and approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority. Thereafter the construction of the development shall
only be carried out in accordance with the approved Plan: The
Construction Management Plan shall include details of:

 

a.   Construction vehicle
numbers, type, routing;

b.   Access arrangements
to the site;

c.   Traffic management
requirements

d.   Construction and
storage compounds (including areas designated for car parking,
loading /unloading and turning areas);

e.   Siting and details
of wheel washing facilities;

f.    Cleaning of
site entrances, site tracks and the adjacent public highway;

g.   Timing of
construction activities (including delivery times and removal of
waste) and to avoid school pick up/drop off times;

h.   Provision of
sufficient on-site parking prior to commencement of construction
activities;

i.
   Post construction
restoration/reinstatement of the working areas and temporary access
to the public highway;

j.    where works
cannot be contained wholly within the site a plan should be
submitted showing the site layout on the highway including extent
of hoarding, pedestrian routes and remaining road width for vehicle
movements;
 
Informatives
 
1.
IN907 - Positive and proactive statement
2.
IN910 - Building Regulations
3.
IN912 - Hours of Construction
4. AN
1) Construction Management Plan (CMP): The purpose of the CMP is to
help developers minimise construction impacts and relates to all
construction activity both on and off
site that impacts on the wider environment. It is intended to be a
live document whereby different stages will be completed
and
submitted for application as the development progresses. A
completed and signed CMP must address the way in which any impacts
associated with the proposed works, and any cumulative impacts of
other nearby construction sites will be mitigated and managed. The
level of detail required in a CMP will depend on the scale and
nature of development.
 
The CMP
would need to include elements of the Construction Logistics and
Community Safety (CLOCS) standards as set out in our Construction
Management template, a copy of which is available on the County
Council's website at:
https:/Iwww.hertfordshire.gov.uklservices/highways-roads-and-pavements/business-and-developer-information/development-managementlhighways-development-management.aspx

purpose:
Double-storey front, side and rear extensions
with internal reconfiguration to provide ancillary facilities
(nursery, cafe, rest room for the deceased, meeting rooms, prayer
halls, sports/events hall, and community spaces) in connection with
the existing place of worship (Use Class F1)
content:
The
committee received a report of the Development Management Lead
which set out the request for extensions to the existing building
and internal reconfiguration to provide ancillary facilities in
connection with the existing place of worship.
 
The
Development Management Lead introduced the report.  She provided background to the site and the
details within the application.  She
explained that the application was not about the use of the
building as a place of worship as this was already permitted under
the existing planning use class F1.  A
transport assessment had been carried out and the site was considered
to be a highly accessible location.  The application included new cycle
parking.  The Highways Authority did not
consider the application would have a significant impact on
traffic, particularly as the hours of worship were outside the
busiest times for traffic.  She advised
that overspill paring on the surrounding area would not be possible
due to the Controlled Parking Zone in the area.  She noted that the applicant would be required to
provide a Travel Plan and the Section
106 agreement would require funds to enable Travel Plan monitoring
to be carried out by the County Council. 
 
The
Development Management Lead then referred to the height of the
building.  She explained that the
maximum height remained unchanged from the existing
building.  The plans had been amended to
remove the windows from the sports hall at first floor
level.  All first
floor windows would be required to have obscured glazing to
prevent any overlooking of the neighbouring garden.  She advised that the nursery had been in place
during the building previous use.  She
was therefore unable to substantiate a refusal.  In summary the application proposed a modest
uplift in floorspace and was in accordance with the Local
Plan.
 
The
Chair noted that the slide showing the distance had referred to 16
metres between the neighbour’s property and the application
site.  However, he noted the resting
place for the deceased was much closer.
 
The
Development Management Lead explained that the distance was between
the neighbour’s property and the two-storey element of the
building. 
 
In
response to a question about the community facilities and whether
they would be open to the wider community, the Development
Management Lead advised that this would be a decision for the
applicant.          
There was also a question about the car parking and monitoring at
busy times.  The Development Management
Lead explained that this was the same level of parking as
existing.  The Highways Authority had
requested the applicant supplied a Travel Plan.  She reminded the committee that the application
was no different to the existing use and could be used at any
time.
 
There
was reference to some of the rooms within the building that seem to
be repeated.  The Development Management
Lead suggested the applicant maybe able
to answer this when he addressed the committee. 
 
There
were no further questions from the committee for the
officer.  The Chair invited Adam Lewis
to speak to the committee against the application.
 
Mr
Lewis advised that he was not ‘objecting’ to the
application.  He lived directly to the
rear of the site.  He said that, like
many local residents, he welcomed the
site being opened, but only if responsibly done.  It would enhance the quality of life for residents
in a residential area.
 
Mr
Lewis explained that there were three areas he would like to
cover.  The first was traffic as this
was a highly congested area at times. 
The ancillary facilities would lead to daytime usage.  Traffic generation was untested.  No Travel Plan had been provided when the
application had been submitted.  The
information regarding traffic and parking was
self-reported.  He asked that the plan
was submitted prior to building works beginning.  The second point was about parking.  The application had proposed an increase in
floorspace and not parking, the two did not align.  He considered reference to the use of public
transport was naïve.  A full Travel
Plan and construction statement was needed, including comparable
sites.  He suggested monitoring could be
required with designated wardens.  His
third concern was about noise, which particularly related to
him.  He felt it was inevitable that
there would be noise from open windows and the nursery.  The officer had acknowledged this in the
report.  There needed to be some form of
mechanical climate control installed. 
The light spill from the first floor
windows would be diffused if obscured glass was installed and not
stopped.  He suggested that some measure
was added as a requirement to prevent the light spilling
out.
 
Mr
Lewis then spoke about the outdoor play space for the
nursery.  He asked whether this could be
relocated to the side of the building rather than the proposed
location.  He had circulated a plan to
the committee earlier in the day to explain his
suggestion.
 
Mr
Lewis thanked the committee for letting him speak to
them.  He asked that in determining the
application members gave full consideration
to the benefits for the applicant and the
residents.
 
The
Chair thanked Mr Lewis. He asked the Development Management Lead if
she could respond to the points raised by Mr Lewis.
 
The
Development Management Lead stressed that the assessment of the
application could not be about the re-use of the building as
existing.  The committee was considering
whether the extra 30% of floorspace created an adverse
harm.  The 32 car parking spaces could
be used at any time.  If there was an
increase in the parking area this would generate an increase in the
number of cars accessing the site. 
There had been no parking survey carried out as the site was in a
Controlled Parking Zone and therefore no overspill was
possible.  Sustainable transport was the
only alternative available.  The
transport statement would always make assumptions about
travel and this was reviewed by the
Highways Authority. 
 
The
Development Management Lead then mentioned about the nose
impact.  Noise would be expected from a
place of worship, which it had been before.  There were no hours of operation in place for the
existing use and therefore it would not be possible to constrain
the hours with this application.  With
regards to the windows and climate control, the officer advised
that the windows could currently be opened and therefore no
restrictions could be imposed.  
Referring to the comments about light spill, the largest windows
had been removed, but members could consider the other windows,
although the existing windows when in use would have created some
light spill.  The officer advised that
the play area could be used at any time; it was not possible to
require this to be relocated.  She
advised members that the applicant had carried out engagement with
the local community.
 
The
Chair thanked the officer for the explanations and then invited
Numan Majeed, the Applicant to speak.  
 
Numan
Majeed thanked the committee for the opportunity to speak to
them.  He explained that he was the
Project Lead on this application.  He
had been born and lived in Watford.  He
also worked locally.  He stressed this
was a locally led initiative and the wider project team were all
local.  The scheme was for the local
community.  He advised that the previous
St Thomas Church had operated more than a place of
worship.  When it closed it became
vacant and derelict.  The application
was to continue the building as a place of worship with additional
ancillary facilities to its purpose.  It
would respect the charm of the surrounding area but be
modern.  The proposal would rationalise
the roof space, which would increase the internal floorspace
without significantly increasing the footprint.  The facilities would respect the historic uses of
the site.  He noted that there had been
a question about the ‘Majlis’ shown in the plan, these
were separate lounges for men and women. 
 
Mr
Majeed then explained the engagement that had been carried out in
the local community.  Residents’
feedback had been incorporated into the plans.  It had then been provided to the Nascot
Residents’ Association for their feedback.  Over 80 residents had supported the
application.  He advised that following
a site visit by officers the rear windows to the sports hall had
been removed.  Additional boundary
fencing would be installed.  The scheme
had continued to evolve based on the advice that had been
received.  He finished by stating that
the application would bring the building back into use as a place
of worship.  The project was locally led
and had been responsive to residents’ views.
 
The
Chair thanked Numan Majeed his presentation.
 
The
Chair invited comments or questions from the committee. 
 
Members
welcomed the building being brought back into use.  It was noted that through discussions changes had
been made to the application.  They had
also heard the suggestions from Mr Lewis about measures for the
windows, hours of operation and location of the play
area.  However, they were also aware
that Mr Lewis had not been resident when the church had previously
operated.  One member commented that
when the church had been in use in the past there had not been a
Controlled Parking Zone operational. 
The applicant was asked to make sure that visitors were aware about
the parking. 
 
Members
were mindful that the premises could be used immediately and it was
not possible to refuse its use or require additional conditions
that were not already in place unless there were significant
reasons.  Previously it had been a
vibrant community space.  There had been
no restrictions on operating times, therefore they could not be
added now.  One member suggested that
there may be more opportunities to discuss the operation of the
building between the applicant and residents.  It was noted that the Travel Plan would be
required before the building became operational.  With regards to parking, reference was made to
other places of worship in the town that were also located in areas
with Controlled Parking Zones in place. 
Worshipers had to make alternative arrangements.  If the level of parking was increased there would
be an increase in traffic to and from the site.  Members sympathised with Mr Lewis and other
neighbours, as this had been a quiet space for some
time.  It would be replaced by a vibrant
building, which could not be controlled through
planning.  In response to a question
about the resting place for the deceased, the Development
Management Lead confirmed that it would be in use 24 hours per
day.
 
Councillor Nembhard said that he was not satisfied with the
scale of the building and the increase by 30%.  He suggested the applicant should work within the
existing footprint.  He considered the
bigger building would lead to an increase in parking and extra
traffic.  The building was also located
in a conservation area.  He knew the
building well as he had visited many times when it had been in
use.  The building needed proper
consideration.  He proposed that the
application should be rejected on the grounds of its density and
scale.
 
It was
noted that the Highways Authority had referred to the 30% increase
as modest.  The Development Management
Lead was asked on what basis this judgement had been
made.
 
The
Development Management Lead explained that the judgement had been
made by the Highways Authority.  It was
recognised the ground floor area had been increased and the resting
place for the dead had been added.  The
sports hall had been enlarged on the guidance of a sporting
organisation.  The
majority of the new space had been created on the first
floor.  The judgement was made by
planning officers and Highways on the intensity of its
use.
 
There
was some discussion about the proposed reason for
refusal.  It was agreed that the
building was within a conservation area.  However, it was necessary to consider whether it
currently made a positive contribution to the area.  Reference was made to St Andrews Church in Nascot,
which was a listed building.  St Thomas
Church did not provide a positive contribution to the area in its
current state.  The activities proposed
would enable the applicant to play a positive role in the local
community.  It was noted the strength of
a planning committee was the ability to have different
views.
 
The
Chair commented that if this had been a new building within the
conservation area he may have had more
sympathy.  However, it was a building
for worship and the use was continuing
as before.  He sympathised with
residents’ concerns about parking,
but did not feel this was a reason the committee could turn
the application down.  The extra uses on
the site would not be grounds to refuse the application
either. 
 
The
Chair noted Councillor Nembhard’s proposal to refuse the
application on the grounds of excessive size of the development and
impact of noise on the community.  He
invited the committee to vote to refuse the application.
 
On
being put to committee the recommendation to refuse the application
was lost.
 
Prior
to the next vote, there was a question about the trees on site the
Tree Preservation Order, particularly during the construction
phase.  The Development Management Lead
assured members that a management plan would be in place and
consideration given to protecting the cedar tree.  It was covered by condition three.
 
The
Chair invited the committee to vote on the officer’s
recommendation.
 
On
being put to committee the application was approved. 
 
The
Chair thanked Mr Lewis for his presentation.  He hoped the representatives from the Mosque would
be able to meet him and discuss his concerns further.
 
Resolved –
 
That,
subject to the completion of a legal agreement under Section 106 of
the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 (as amended) to secure the
following heads of terms, planning permission be granted subject to
the conditions listed below:

1.         Time

3.         Tree

No development, including demolition works, shall commence until

No development shall commence until full details of a hard

No development shall commence until full details of a soft

Authority. The soft landscaping shall be completed no later than

6.        
Materials

           
No development shall commence until details and samples of the
materials to be used for all the external finishes of the
development hereby approved, including all external walls, all

7.         Construction
Management Plan (HCC Highways)

has been submitted to and approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority. The Construction Method Statement shall include elements
of the CLOCS standards as set out in the Highway Authorities
Construction Management template. Thereafter the construction of
the development shall only be carried out in accordance with the
approved plan. The Construction Statement shall include details
of:

a.   Construction vehicle
numbers, type, routing;

b.   Access arrangements
to the site;

c.   Traffic management
requirements

d.   Construction and
storage compounds (including areas designated for car parking,
loading / unloading and turning areas);

e.   Siting and details
of wheel washing facilities;

f.    Cleaning of
site entrances, site tracks and the adjacent public highway;

g.   Timing of
construction activities (including delivery times and removal of
waste) and to avoid school pick up/drop off times;
 

8.         Travel
Plan

           
At least 3 months prior to the first occupation or use of the
approved development a detailed Travel Plan for the site shall be
submitted to and approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority in consultation with the Highways Authority. The approved
Travel Plan Statement shall be implemented in accordance with the
timetable and target contained in therein and shall continue to be
implemented as long as any part of the
development is occupied subject to approved modifications agreed by
the Local Planning Authority in consultation with the Highway
Authority as part of the annual review. Page 39

 

9.         Access and
Egress

           
Prior to the first occupation of the development hereby permitted,
the vehicular and pedestrian (and cyclist) access to, and egress
from, the adjoining public highway shall be limited to the access
shown on drawing number DPV/BD/P/014 (Proposed Site Plan Detail)
only. Any other access or egresses hall be permanently closed, and
the footway and kerbline shall be
reinstated in accordance with a detailed scheme to be approved in
writing by the Local Planning Authority in consultation with the
highway authority.

 

10.       Site arrangements (HCC
Highways)

           
Prior to the first use of the development hereby permitted, the
proposed onsite car and cycle parking, servicing and turning area
shall be implemented in accordance with approved drawing numbers
DPB/BD/P1014 (proposed Site Plan Detail) and retained thereafter
available for that specific use.

 

11.       Cycle storage

           
No part of the development shall be occupied until full details of
the cycle storage has been submitted to and approved in writing by
the Local Planning Authority. Details shall include a security
scheme for the parking of cycles and the
type of cycle stands must also be clarified and designed in line
with standards contained in the DfT'S
LTN1/20. The storage approved under this condition shall be
installed and made available for use prior to the occupation of any
part of the development and shall be retained
at all times for cycle storage only and shall not be used
for any other purpose.

 

12.       Bin storage

           
No part of the development shall be occupied until the bin storage
has been provided for the use of staff and visitors, in accordance
with the approved drawings. These facilities shall be retained at all times.

 

13.       Obscurely glazed
windows

           
The proposed first floor windows in the north (rear) facing
elevation of the development shall be permanently fitted with
obscure glass and the part of the window, less than 1.7m above
internal floor level, shall be permanently fixed closed.

 

14.       Plant and
Machinery

           
Prior to the first occupation of the development hereby approved,
details of all new external plant or machinery shall be submitted
to and approved in writing by the Local Planning Authority. In
respect of any plant that emits sound, details shall include
appropriate noise assessments carried out and undertaken by
appropriately qualified technical consultants. The noise assessment
shall include details of any necessary mitigation, which shall be
installed prior to the plant being brought into
operation.

 

15.       Energy and
Sustainability

           
No part of the development shall be occupied until the energy
saving and renewable energy measures detailed within the approved
Energy and Sustainability Statement (prepared by MACH Group Energy
dated 10 Oct 2025) are incorporated as detailed into the approved
development.

 
Informatives
 

1.         IN907 –
Positive proactive statement to grant

           
In dealing with this application, Watford Borough Council has
considered the proposal in a positive and proactive manner having
regard to the policies of the development plan, the National
Planning Policy Framework and other material planning
considerations, and in accordance with the Town and Country
Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015
(as amended).

 

2.         IN910 –
Building Regulations

           
This permission does not remove the need to obtain any separate
consent, which may be required under the Buildings Act 1984 or
other building control legislation. Nor does it override any
private rights which any person may have relating to the land
affected by this decision. To find out more information and for
advice as to whether a Building Regulations application will be
required please visit www.watfordbuildingcontrol.com.

 

3.         IN912 –
Hours of Construction

           
You are advised of the need to comply with the provisions of The
Control of Pollution Act 1974, The Health and Safety at Work Act
1974, The Clean Air Act 1993 and The Environmental Protection Act
1990.

 

           
In order to minimise impact of noise,
any works associated with the development which are audible at the
site boundary should be restricted to the following
hours:

           
- Monday to Friday 8am to 6pm

           
- Saturdays 8am to 1pm

           
- Noisy work is prohibited on Sundays and bank holidays

 

           
Instructions should be given to ensure that vehicles and plant
entering and leaving the site comply with the stated hours of
work.

 

           
Further details for both the applicant and those potentially
affected by construction noise can be found on the Council's
website at:
https://www.watford.gov.uk/info/20010/your_environment/188/neighbour_complaints_%E2%80%93_construction_noise

 

4.         IN913 –
Community Infrastructure Levy Liability

           
Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) - Your development may be
liable for CIL payments and you are
advised to contact the CIL Officer (cil@watford.gov.uk) for
clarification with regard to this. If
your development is CIL liable, even if you have been granted
exemption from the levy, please be advised that before commencement
of any works it is a requirement under Regulation 67 of The
Community Infrastructure Levy Regulations 2010 (as amended) that
CIL form 6 (Commencement Notice) must be completed, returned and
acknowledged by Watford Borough Council before building works
start. Failure to do so will mean you lose the right to payment by
instalments (where applicable), and a surcharge will be imposed.
However, please note that a Commencement Notice is not required for
residential extensions IF relief has been applied for and
granted.

 

5.         Highway
Works

           
All works required to be undertaken on the highway network will
require an Agreement with the Highway Authority. Before commencing
the development the applicant shall
contact HCC Highways Development Management, County Hall, Pegs
Lane, Hertford, SG13 8DN to obtain their permission and
requirements. This is to ensure any work undertaken in the highway
is constructed in accordance with the Highway Authority's
specification and by a contractor who is authorised to work in the
public highway.

content:
The
following motion had been proposed by Councillor Peter Kloss and
seconded by Mayor Peter Taylor:

 
“This council notes that:
 
Elections for Mayor of Watford and 12 Watford Borough Council
ward seats are due to occur on 7th May 2026.
 
In light of the
proposed changes in local government in Hertfordshire, the
government has asked local government authorities if they would
like to cancel these elections.
 
The
final decision on the future unitary model of local government in
Hertfordshire is not anticipated until summer 2026, with new
unitary councils not expected to have their full powers until
Spring 2028 at the earliest.
 
This
council believes that:
· Residents
must have the opportunity to choose their elected representatives
in accordance with legal requirements, and their expectations and
understanding of the established electoral process.
· A decision
to cancel the 2026 local elections would be deeply undemocratic,
resulting in an incumbent Mayor or Councillor elected in 2022
serving for at least 6 years, rather than the 4 years voters
understood at the time.
 
The
council urges the government to:
· Proceed
with local elections in Watford and elsewhere nationally to allow
residents the right to exercise their democratic rights.
· Maintain
and support the current model of local government democracy until
specific decisions on a new unitary model are made.
 
Council
resolves to:
· Ask the
Elected Mayor of Watford to write to the Secretary of State for
Housing, Communities and Local Government to express that local
democracy is important for our residents and urge that our local
elections scheduled for May 2026 proceed as
planned.”
 
Prior
to the meeting Councillor Kloss, seconded by Mayor Taylor proposed
an amendment to the motion as published.  The amendment was as follows:
 
“The council notes that:

Elections for Mayor of Watford and 12 Watford Borough Council
ward seats are due to occur on 7th May 2026.
In light of the
proposed changes in local government in Hertfordshire, the
government has asked local government authorities if they would
like to cancel these elections.
Watford Borough Council made its position clear that it does not
want elections cancelled, and the government has since confirmed
they will proceed.
The
final decision on the future unitary model of local government in
Hertfordshire is not anticipated until summer 2026, with new
unitary councils not expected to have their full powers until
Spring 2028 at the earliest.  

 
This
council believes that:

Residents must have the opportunity to choose their elected
representatives in accordance with legal requirements, and their
expectations and understanding of the established electoral
process.
A
decision to cancel the 2026 local elections would have been be deeply undemocratic, resulting
in an incumbent Mayor or Councillor elected in 2022 serving for at
least 6 years, rather than the 4 years voters understood at the
time.

 
The
council urges the government confirms its commitment to:

Proceed with local elections in Watford and elsewhere nationally
to allow residents the right to exercise their democratic
rights.


Maintain and support the current model of local government
democracy until specific decisions on a new unitary model are
made.

 
Council
resolves to:

·       
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to write to the
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government to
express that local democracy is important for our residents and
confirm urge that our
local elections scheduled for May 2026 will proceed as
planned.”
 
Councillor Bell, on behalf of the Labour Group, accepted the
amended motion, which became the substantive motion.
 
Members
spoke to the motion.
 
Resolved –
 
The
council notes that:

Elections for Mayor of Watford and 12 Watford Borough Council
ward seats are due to occur on 7th May 2026.
In light of the
proposed changes in local government in Hertfordshire, the
government has asked local government authorities if they would
like to cancel these elections.
Watford Borough Council made its position clear that it does not
want elections cancelled, and the government has since confirmed
they will proceed.
The
final decision on the future unitary model of local government in
Hertfordshire is not anticipated until summer 2026, with new
unitary councils not expected to have their full powers until
Spring 2028 at the earliest.  

 
This
council believes that:

Residents must have the opportunity to choose their elected
representatives in accordance with legal requirements, and their
expectations and understanding of the established electoral
process.
A
decision to cancel the 2026 local elections would have been deeply
undemocratic, resulting in an incumbent Mayor or Councillor elected
in 2022 serving for at least 6 years, rather than the 4 years
voters understood at the time.

 
The
council confirms its commitment to:

Proceed with local elections in Watford and elsewhere nationally
to allow residents the right to exercise their democratic
rights.


Maintain and support the current model of local government
democracy until specific decisions on a new unitary model are
made.

 
Council
resolves to:

·       
Ask the Elected Mayor of Watford to write to the
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government to
express that local democracy is important for our residents and
confirm that our local elections scheduled for May 2026 will
proceed as planned.
topline: The Council has decided to proceed with the local elections scheduled for May 2026, affirming the importance of local democracy and residents' right to choose their representatives.

content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Chief Finance Officer which set out the
draft Charging Policy for 2026/27 and the proposed fees and
charges.
 
The
Mayor invited Councillor Begum to introduce the report.
 
Councillor Begum informed members that the report included the
draft Charging Policy for 2026/27 and the schedule of charges for
2026/27.  In preparing the fees and
charges officers were mindful of the Consumer Price Index, which in
April 2025 was 3.50%.  The majority of the charges would be introduced from
1 February 2026, although there were some exceptions including
parking permits from 1 June 2026 and the garden waste subscription
would apply from 1 September.  The
recommendations included some delegations to officers for leisure
service fees and Market Licence fees, in consultation with the
Portfolio Holder.  She added that some
fees were set by central Government. 
Finally, she noted that the licensing fees had been considered by
the Licensing Committee at its recent meeting.
 
The
Mayor thanked the Portfolio Holder for her presentation and opened
the meeting to questions or comments from other
members.  He invited Councillor Khan,
Chair of the Finance Scrutiny Committee to speak.
 
Councillor Khan informed Cabinet that the scrutiny committee
recognised the need to review the officer’s report and
recommendations.  The scrutiny committee
had focussed its discussion on three key topics, affordability and
fairness, ensuring the increases did not affect people
disproportionately, particularly those on lower incomes or
protected characteristics.  The second
area focussed on benchmarking and asked officers to ensure proposed
fees were evidence based and reflected the cost of the
service.  This was to ensure no fees
were solely driven by income targets. 
The third area was communication.  This
was to ensure that charges were clearly explained to businesses and
residents.  Also the scrutiny committee considered the way the
fees and charges were spread across the year.  The scrutiny committee had noted the report and
did not raise any fundamental objections to the fees and
charges.  The scrutiny committee would
continue its ongoing monitoring throughout the year.
 
The
Mayor thanked Councillor Khan for the scrutiny committee’s
feedback.  Members had held lots of
discussions about the fees and charges. 
As there were no further comments or questions, the Mayor moved the
recommendations in the report.
 
Resolved –
 
that
Cabinet recommends to Council:
 

1.         to approve the
draft Charging Policy 2026/27 at Appendix 1 to the
report.

 

2.         to approve the
proposed fees and charges for introduction from 1 February 2026 and
other dates as specified at Appendix 2.

 

3.         to approve to
delegate authority to set the leisure service fees to the Director
of Sustainability, Environment and Communities, in consultation
with the Portfolio Holder. 

 

4.         to
approve to delegate authority to set the charges in respect of
Market licence fees to the Director of Sustainability, Environment
and Communities, in consultation with the Portfolio
Holder.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to recommend the approval of the draft Charging Policy for 2026/27 and proposed fees and charges.

purpose:
Updates on Delivery Plan, KPIs and Key
Corporate Strategies
content:
Cabinet
received a report of the Associate Director of Customer and
Corporate Services, Delivery Support Lead, Intelligence Performance
and Improvement Lead and Community Commissioning Lead.  The report set out an update which reflected the
positive outcomes that had been achieved over the first two
quarters of 2025/26.
 
The Mayor introduced the report and thanked the
officers for the wealth of information. 
It was good to be able to see the progress that had been
made.  He mentioned some of the
highlights, including the River Colne festival which had attracted
500 visitors; the 22 businesses who had been awarded the Watford
Business pledge; the improvement works at the Central Leisure
Centre.  He also informed Cabinet that
the number of rough sleepers had fallen.
 
He invited members to comment or ask
questions.
 
Councillor Pattinson referred to some of those
elements within her portfolio of Housing and Wellbeing.  She noted the Mayor had referred to homelessness
and it was good to see these were now in single
figures.  There had been an increase in
temporary accommodation in quarter 2. 
She noted that there were limited move-on options in social and
affordable housing.  She added that the
latest statistics showed this was below forecast, which was
positive.   The Ascot Road
development lettings had a positive impact on the temporary
accommodation figures, although it was noted that levels were
rising again, which was due to lack of stock and demand
rising.  She said that prevention was
the way forward.  She referred to the
forthcoming landlord event; there had been two previous successful
landlord events.  This enabled the
council to work with private sector landlords.  She recognised there were pressures in Housing but
with the prevention work there was a clear direction of
travel.
 
The Mayor said that the previous landlord event
that he had attended had been excellent.  He invited Councillor Hill to
speak.
 
Councillor Hill referred to the Customer Service
Centre and the significant improvement in this area.  This was the way in which many residents contacted
the council.  There had been an
improvement in the performance of response to
complaints. 
 
The Mayor invited Councillor Bell to
speak.
 
Councillor Bell referred to Councillor
Pattinson’s comments and the temporary accommodation
presentation to Finance Scrutiny Committee.   He recognised the good work done by the
Housing team on temporary accommodation, but the report showed this
was still under target, although he acknowledged the Portfolio
Holder’s comments.  He asked the
Portfolio Holder if she could explain about the below target
performance for homeless relief cases closed with a successful
outcome.
 
Councillor Pattinson confirmed that this was
below target.  The service had focused
on preventing homelessness.  It was
hoped the statistics would improve in the next quarter; the
monitoring from quarter 2 onwards indicated it was moving in the
right direction.
 
Councillor Bell then referred to the customer
complaints response times, as this was still under
target.  He mentioned the comments about
in the report about Council Tax.
 
The Associate Director for Corporate and Customer
Services explained that this statistic was about formal written
complaints.  The target to respond to
complaints within the 10-day deadline was 100%.  However, it was recognised that some complaints
were very complex and required more time to sufficiently
investigate.  In line with the
council’s Complaints Policy, services contacted the
complainant and asked for an extension to the 10-day deadline to
enable a detailed response to be provided. 
 
The Mayor noted that on the page that Councillor
bel had referred to, 12 of the measures had made improvement and
only one had declined.  Overall, there
had been lots of progress in different areas.  He invited Cabinet to vote on the
recommendations.
 
Resolved –
 

1.         that Cabinet
notes the progress update within the report relating to:
 

·      
the Council Plan 2022-26 and Delivery Plan 2024 -26
(Appendix A)

·      
the external key performance indicator results for
Quarter 2 of 2025/26 (Appendix B)

·      
the Voluntary Sector Commissioning Framework metrics
for Quarter 2 of 2025/26 (Appendix C)

·      
the council’s key corporate strategies
(Appendix D)

·      
the Ombudsman decisions for Quarter 2 of
2025/26
 

2.         that Cabinet
notes the progress updates relating to the Delivery Plan, key
performance indicators and key corporate strategies will be
presented to Overview and Scrutiny Committee in January
2026.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations based on a progress update report showing positive outcomes in various areas for the first two quarters of 2025/26.

content:

Bike contract to be extended for a further five years with a
rolling break clause beginning 2029.  It
was noted that the appendix to the report was exempt from
publication as it contained commercially sensitive
information.
 
Councillor Stotesbury introduced the report.  He said that the proposal had been developed
as a result of Local Government
Reform.  He welcomed the re-injection
into the local service.  This was a
successful scheme in Watford.  The
council had been bold in its introduction of e-bikes. 220 new
e-bikes would be introduced and 80 pedal bikes.  The council had opted for both types of bikes to
provide customers with a choice.  
Since its introductions the scheme had extended into Three Rivers
and Hertsmere.  The company had enhanced
its social value initiatives by introducing free hours for job
seekers, cycling by prescription and as part of the community
champion project. 
 
The
Mayor welcomed the introduction of new bikes.  He asked when the bikes would be available in
Watford.
 
Councillor Stotesbury responded that it was hoped that some
would be made available soon.  The Chief
Operating Officer cautioned that it would depend on the supply
chain.  The new fleet was expected by 1
April 2026.
 
The
Mayor thanked Councillor Stotesbury and officers.  He noted that there were no questions about the
Part B appendix.  He invited Cabinet to
note the report.
 
Resolved –
 
That
the exemption as detailed in the appendix is noted.
